name: Tomato
description: A sun-loving fruit with thousands of varieties in red, black, pink, green or striped, from blueberry-sized wild tomatoes to beefsteaks weighing a kilo. It reached Sweden in the 1600s as 'love apples', grown only as an ornamental.
howToEat: Keep ripe tomatoes at room temperature, as the fridge kills their aroma. Green tomatoes can be fried in olive oil with lemon, or pickled. Only the fruit is eaten; the leaves and stems are poisonous.

events.note: Sow late March, 6–8 weeks before planting out — earlier just makes leggy plants. Warm house; the conservatory's still too cold.
Early April at the latest — still in time for the greenhouse move.
Into the unheated greenhouse once nights stay above ~10°C there — usually late May, early June in a cold spring. Bury the stem deep.
Ripening fast in the greenhouse.
Pick everything before the greenhouse gets frost (often late September). Green ones ripen indoors.

name: Pepper
description: A bushy plant from South America, 50–100 cm tall, whose fruits contain the hot compound capsaicin. As a rule, the smaller and more pointed the fruit, the hotter it is.
howToEat: Pick green or ripe, and dry by hanging the plants upside down or laying split fruits on a mesh. Scrape out the seeds and white membranes, which are very hot, and wash your hands afterwards.

events.note: Longest season of all — germinate, then keep in the warm house.
Last chance to start if you didn't in January — warm-lovers, keep them in the house.
Early June, once the greenhouse stays warm at night — chillies sulk below ~12°C.
First fruits ripening.
Pick everything remaining before the greenhouse gets frost.

name: Pepper
description: A bushy plant from South America, 50–100 cm tall, closely related to chilli but with sweet, mild fruits. Swedes only started putting it on their sandwiches a few decades ago.
howToEat: Pick fruits as they come, either unripe when green or yellow, or ripe when usually red. Slice it raw onto sandwiches.

events.note: Start from February — a long season, but they don't need a January start like chillies.
Last chance to start — warm-lovers, keep them in the house.
Early June, once the greenhouse stays warm at night.
First peppers — pick some green to keep the plant setting more.
Pick everything remaining before the greenhouse gets frost.

name: Cucumber
description: A trailing, tendril-climbing plant with mostly green, sometimes white fruits that are almost all water. Outdoor pickling cucumbers are short, plump and bumpy, while slicing cucumbers are long and smooth; there is even a round, yellow apple cucumber.
howToEat: Pick small, firm outdoor cucumbers for pickling. Young ones are also good in salad, perhaps peeled, and excellent in tzatziki. Slicing and apple cucumbers are eaten fresh.

events.note: Sow late April, 3–4 weeks before planting out; warm-lovers, so germinate and grow on in the warm house.
Early June — cucumbers are the most cold-sensitive crop here. Give them strings to climb.
Pick regularly to keep them coming.

name: Pumpkin
description: Pumpkins and winter squash have extremely hard skins, yellow flesh rich in carotene and long trailing vines. World-record pumpkins usually belong to this group, and the fig-leaf pumpkin's melon-sized fruits can keep for a year.
howToEat: Let the stalk harden before picking, dry the fruit indoors in a warm room, then store it at room temperature or a bit cooler right through winter. Fig-leaf pumpkin is used for candying in some countries.

events.note: Start late April, 4 weeks before planting out.
Plant out early June, after the frost risk, once hardened off. Fleece for the first week.
Cut before the first frost (often late September), with a long stalk. Cure indoors somewhere warm for 1–2 weeks — the autumn sun is too weak.

name: Squash
description: Summer squash (courgette or zucchini) grows as a bush with thin-skinned, white-fleshed fruits in many shapes and colours. The author rates the striped Costata Romanesco as the most flavourful summer squash there is.
howToEat: Eat the fruits fresh, picked at no more than 20-25 cm long; after that they are not good. They only keep for a few weeks.

events.note: Start late April with the pumpkins.
Plant out early June, after the frost risk, once hardened off. Fleece for the first week.
Summer squash from August — pick small and often.
Cut winter squash before the first frost. Cure indoors somewhere warm for 1–2 weeks.

name: Onion
description: The ordinary cooking onion, yellow, red or white, descended from a wild onion in the mountains of Turkmenistan. Variants include small pearl onions, silver-skinned onions and small white pickling onions.
howToEat: Dried onions keep for months at room temperature, longer if dry and near 0°C. Eat any that flower first, as they won't store. A little of the green tops can be used like spring onion.

events.note: Sow from seed for big bulbs by late summer — germinate warm, then grow on cool & bright in the conservatory so they don't get leggy.
Continue sowing; germinate warm, grow on cool in the conservatory.
Plant out seedlings late April to mid May, once the soil has thawed.
Use as they size up.
Lift when the tops fall over; cure somewhere dry and airy until the skins are papery.
Book's safest method (p. 326): push sets in as soon as the soil is workable, a quarter showing. Red onion 1–2 weeks later or it may bolt.
Overwintering sets — early September so they root before the freeze. Riskier than garlic; only with reliable snow cover.
Use as they size up.
Lift when the tops fall over; cure somewhere dry and airy until the skins are papery.

name: Onion
description: A slimmer form of Welsh onion developed by Asian breeders, about 50-60 cm tall with a rich, mild onion flavour. Some varieties have long white stems or purple colouring.
howToEat: The Chinese eat it almost every day, both raw and cooked; its mild flavour suits all kinds of dishes.

events.note: Book method (p. 331): start indoors, about 10 seeds per pot so each pot grows into a clump.
Plant out the whole clump once the soil has warmed. Clumps 10 cm apart.
Optional: sow direct in rows, 2 cm apart. Works, but the harvest comes later than from indoor-started clumps.
Pull stems one at a time as needed. Earth up the stems for white, tender bases.

name: Leek
description: A tall onion with a thick white stem, developed from a wild leek that grows as a weed in Mediterranean vineyards. It only caught on in Sweden well into the 1900s.
howToEat: Harvest in late autumn and store at 0-2°C.

events.note: Sow in modules; germinate warm, then move to the conservatory to keep them sturdy.
Continue sowing; grow on cool in the conservatory.
Plant out late May to end of June — drop into deep dibbed holes and water in. Later and they run out of season.
Lift as needed. Leeks take frost, but lift the rest before the ground freezes solid (usually November).

name: Garlic
description: A bulb made of cloves, grown in medieval Swedish monastery gardens as medicine rather than food. Freshly harvested garlic has an almost addictive smell and taste; it grows wild in Asia and the ancient Egyptians loved it.
howToEat: Dry the bulbs in the sun and store them hanging, often braided, somewhere dry. In spring, snip a little of the mild garlicky leaves for salad; the small bulbils on the flower stalk are edible too.

events.note: Late September — gives the cloves time to root before the freeze.
Early October at the latest — cloves pointy end up, 5cm deep, then mulch.
Snap off the flower stalks (scapes) to boost bulb size — and eat them.
Lift late July to early August when the lower leaves yellow. Cure somewhere dry and airy.

name: Carrot
description: Sweden's favourite root vegetable. The first carrots came from Afghanistan and were dark purple; white and yellow ones followed, and the orange carrot, rich in beta-carotene, was bred in Holland in the 1600s.
howToEat: Early carrots are the tastiest, and tender thinnings are a treat. Store later carrots cool and moist in damp sand, where they keep all winter in a root cellar.

events.note: Early carrots — sow in a deep container in the conservatory. They hate being moved, so they grow on where they're sown.
Late April, once the soil has thawed — sow under fleece to keep carrot fly off.
Succession sow every few weeks for a steady supply.
Early July at the latest for autumn roots — later ones stay tiny.
Early carrots from the conservatory.
Pull as they size up.
Lift the rest before the ground freezes and store in boxes of damp sand.

name: Parsnip
description: A long, pale root from southern Europe that copes with frost and rough weather like a true northerner. It reached the Nordic countries in the 1400s.
howToEat: A much-loved soup vegetable that tastes best after frost. Store like carrots. The leaves can be used as a herb, fresh, dried or frozen.

events.note: Late April to May, once the soil has thawed — slow to germinate, so be patient and keep moist.
Sweeter after frost — but lift and store before the ground freezes hard (a thick straw mulch buys a few weeks).

name: Beetroot
description: A sweet root descended from wild sea beet, grown by the Romans. Besides the classic red there are yellow, white and red-and-white striped beets, all sweeter than the red.
howToEat: Pickled, or used in veggie burgers, salads and soups; the juice is prized for health. Long beets are easy to slice and pickle, and young leaves can be cooked like chard.

events.note: Direct sow once the soil is ~8°C; thin clusters to one seedling.
Continue for autumn roots.
Early July only, for a late crop.
Golf-ball to tennis-ball size is sweetest.
Lift the rest before heavy frost and store in damp sand.

name: Radish
description: Spring's first fresh vegetable: a quick, crisp little root, usually red and round but also long, white, purple or pink. It came from East Asia and reached Swedish manor gardens in the 1600s.
howToEat: Young leaves can go in soups and salads. The spicy seed pods are eaten raw or, even better, stir-fried. Radishes keep two weeks in the fridge.

events.note: Sow direct in the frost-free conservatory — slow in the cold, but the first fresh crop of the year.
Sow direct in the conservatory now — outdoors is still frozen.
Late April, once the soil has thawed — quick 25–30 day crop; sow little and often.
Keep the succession going.
Small sowings only — long midsummer days and heat make radishes bolt and go woody. Part shade helps.
Best autumn sowing — shortening days, no bolting.
First radishes from the conservatory.
Pull about 4 weeks after sowing, before they go woody.

name: Turnip
description: An early turnip that is smaller, juicier and milder than the old autumn turnips. In the Middle Ages growing turnips was compulsory.
howToEat: Used the same way as swede. Pick them no bigger than tennis balls while tender and mild; they keep a few weeks in damp sand.

events.note: Direct sow for quick summer roots.
Sow for autumn roots and to store.
Pull golf-ball size for eating fresh; lift the rest before the ground freezes.

name: Kohlrabi
description: An odd member of the cabbage family: we eat the swollen, ball-shaped stem that grows above ground. Pale green or purple outside and white inside, with a mild, sweet cabbage taste and unbeatable crunch.
howToEat: Peel it and eat it raw or boiled, both equally good. It stores in a cellar like other roots, or for nearly two months in the fridge.

events.note: Fast and hardy — direct sow a short row every few weeks.
Pick at tennis-ball size, before they get woody.

name: Pea
description: The classic garden pea grown for its green peas, like the ones we now buy frozen. Round-seeded shelling peas are the hardiest, while wrinkled marrowfat types are sweeter.
howToEat: Shell the peas and eat them when pods and peas are fully grown but still fresh green, which is when they are at their sweetest.

events.note: Late April to May, once the snow has gone and the soil has thawed. Support with twiggy sticks.
Pick young and often to keep them producing.

name: Pea
description: A sugar pea bred to be fleshier, staying tender and string-free for longer. The variety Sugar Snap is described as stringless and incredibly juicy.
howToEat: Eat the whole pod, which only gets juicier and tastier as the peas fill out. It is the best kind of pea for freezing.

events.note: Late April to May with twiggy support, once the soil has thawed.
Pick regularly for tender, sweet pods.

name: Bean
description: A sturdy, almost metre-tall bean with snow-white flowers and pods holding four to nine large, flat beans. Grown in Sweden since the 1200s, and its protein content is nearly as high as soy.
howToEat: Eat the beans fresh when bright green but well developed, with no need to peel them, or let them dry on the plant to store over winter. Fresh, blanched beans freeze well.

events.note: Very hardy — sow as soon as the soil has thawed. (Skip autumn sowing — they don't survive a Swedish winter.)
Best picked small and tender.

name: Bean
description: Also called haricots verts, this bean from the South American bean family is grown for its tender green pods. Yellow wax beans and purple beans are close relatives, and purple pods turn green when cooked.
howToEat: Pick the pods before the seeds start to swell. They are cooked whole or in pieces, and freeze well after blanching. Never eat the pods raw; raw beans are poisonous.

events.note: Frost-tender — wait for early June and soil above ~12°C.
Early July only — later sowings won't crop before the first frost.
Pick young and often; stop at the first frost.

name: Bean
description: A climbing bean with long twining vines and showy red, white or salmon-pink flowers. In Sweden it is mostly grown as an ornamental, but in England it is a much-loved eating bean.
howToEat: Pick the pods young, before the beans swell, as older pods get stringy. Slice them crosswise or lengthwise and boil, or blanch and freeze them like French beans. Never eat the pods or beans raw; raw beans are poisonous.

events.note: Sow in deep pots mid May for a head start — runners need the whole season.
Plant out early June, after the frost risk, at the foot of tall supports.
Pick often while the pods are young; stop at the first frost.

name: Bean
description: A bean grown for the seeds inside the pod rather than the pod itself, like Swedish brown beans. The Italian borlotti has beautiful red-speckled pods and fresh beans of gourmet quality.
howToEat: Let the beans ripen and dry, dry them indoors a few more days and store them in lidded jars over winter. They can also be eaten fresh, and very young pods are edible too. Always cook the beans well, fresh or dried; raw beans are poisonous. Soak dried beans first.

events.note: Early June, soil above ~12°C — they need the whole season to dry.
Leave the pods to dry on the plant; pick before the first frost and finish drying indoors.

name: Broccoli
description: Modern broccoli forms one large, compact central head, followed by small side shoots all autumn. Older bushy types give lots of small flower shoots, and some varieties have purple shoots with a strong cabbage flavour.
howToEat: Eat the tight green bud heads before any yellow shows, and the side shoots as they come. Frozen broccoli is hugely popular, and on some varieties the long tender stems are eaten too.

events.note: Germinate warm, then grow on cool & bright in the conservatory for stocky module plants.
Sow a second batch in modules for autumn heads.
Plant out once hardened off — brassicas take a light frost. Net against cabbage white butterflies.
Plant out the second batch.
Cut the main head while tight, then pick the side shoots.
Autumn heads from the second batch — they take light frost.

name: Cabbage
description: The classic cabbage with a firm head; King Gustav Vasa grew tons of it in Stockholm. Summer cabbage, including the small, fast-growing pointed cabbage, is for eating fresh, while autumn and winter cabbage are for storing.
howToEat: Eat summer and pointed cabbage fresh; the fresh leaves are a lovely early treat. Store autumn and winter cabbage cool (around 0°C) and airy, ideally hung root-up in a root cellar.

events.note: Start warm, move to the conservatory once up — warm + dim makes brassicas leggy.
Plant out once hardened off. Net against cabbage whites.
Cut when firm. Cabbages take frost.

name: Cauliflower
description: A refined form of broccoli that Mark Twain called "broccoli with a college education". It was grown in the Middle East 2,000 years ago, and early heads were both purple and white.
howToEat: Eat the head before it starts to split. It keeps for a couple of weeks in the fridge.

events.note: Start warm, move to the conservatory once up — warm + dim makes brassicas leggy.
Plant out once hardened off. Net against cabbage whites.
Cut while the curds are tight. Cauliflowers don't take frost, so cut before it.

name: Kale
description: A leafy cabbage that forms no head, most often green and curly, but also smooth-leaved or wine-red. It has more vitamins and minerals than other cabbages and has been grown since ancient times.
howToEat: Pick the outer leaves as needed; really young leaves are good in salad. It tastes better after a touch of frost, and you can even dig leaves out of the snow in winter.

events.note: Sow in modules; germinate warm, grow on cool in the conservatory.
Plant out module-grown kale.
Early July at the latest — August is too late for a short season.
Pick lower leaves. Frost makes kale sweeter, and it keeps going until the snow buries it.

name: Pak choi
description: Pak choi has been the star of Chinese vegetable growing since the 400s. It forms a vase-shaped head of leaves on thick, often chalk-white stems, and tastes better than chard.
howToEat: The leaves and stems are tender raw, boiled or stir-fried. Use young leaves in salad, add to soups near the end, and stir-fry the stems a minute before the leaves.

events.note: Sow from mid July — before that, the long midsummer days make pak choi bolt.
Best sowing as it cools.
Cut whole heads or pick leaves; they take light frost.

name: Mizuna
description: An easy Asian leaf green forming handsome clumps of deeply cut leaves on thin white stems, with a fresh, crisp texture and mild cabbage-mustard flavour.
howToEat: Use it raw in salads, in soups and stews, stir-fried or in pies. Keeps a week in a plastic bag somewhere cool, or blanch and freeze.

events.note: Sow from late July — it bolts in long midsummer days, and thrives as it cools.
Cut-and-come-again; takes light frost.

name: Mustard greens
description: A relative of mustard grown for its leaves, which come curly, frilly, round, green or red. Mildly peppery, though older plants and those in flower get much hotter.
howToEat: Both stems and leaves are used in cooking, while tender young leaves are best for salad. It also works stir-fried or in soups.

events.note: Sow from late July — it bolts in long midsummer days, and gets milder as it cools.
Pick leaves young for salads, bigger for cooking; takes light frost.

name: Chard
description: Chard descends from wild sea beet and has large leaves and broad stems in white, yellow, orange or red. It reached the Nordic countries in the 1400s.
howToEat: Use the leaves like spinach or to make stuffed leaf rolls. Cut off the stems and cook them separately, a bit like asparagus. Red stems turn green when boiled.

events.note: Half-hardy — sow from May (not April) for a big summer supply.
Sow more rows for autumn.
Early July for autumn picking. It won't survive the winter outside.
Pick outer leaves as needed until the hard frosts.

name: Lettuce
description: Lettuce comes in many types: soft butterhead, fast loose-leaf, crisp iceberg, batavia, and romaine (cos) with big, crunchy, flavourful leaves. Iceberg was only grown in Sweden after World War II.
howToEat: Eat fresh in salads. Store in a sealed plastic bag in the fridge, but make sure it isn't wet or it can rot.

events.note: Book method (p. 274): sow direct from late April, once the soil is workable. Seed germinates from 5 °C.
Optional head start in modules: germinate, then grow on cool in the conservatory; it hates being warm and dark.
Plant out module plants late April to May, at the same depth as in the pot (deeper and they rot). Fleece at first.
Keep sowing little and often. Seed won't germinate at 20 °C or more: sow in the afternoon and water with ice-cold water.
Last outdoor sowing, fast varieties for autumn. Outdoor lettuce won't survive a Stockholm winter; for winter leaves see Winter salad.
Cut from late May until the hard frosts. Water evenly: drought makes lettuce bitter.

name: Winter salad
description: Our own mix of hardy salad leaves, grown in the frost-free conservatory for fresh leaves from autumn through winter into spring.
howToEat: Cut young leaves for salads.

events.note: Sow your first salads direct in the frost-free conservatory — slow, but the first fresh leaves of spring.
Cut-and-come-again; sow direct in the conservatory.
Sow in the frost-free conservatory as nights cool — it'll crop right through the cold.
Cut sparingly from the frost-free conservatory — in deep winter they hold rather than grow.
Still pickable from the conservatory — growth begins to wake as light returns.
Last cuttings from the autumn sowings before they bolt.
Fresh leaves from the February and March sowings.
First cuttings from the September sowings, late in the month.
Keep cutting from the frost-free conservatory as the outdoor crops finish.
Cut sparingly from the frost-free conservatory — in deep winter they hold rather than grow.

name: Spinach
description: Originally from Asia but now thought of as European, spinach has leaves rich in minerals and vitamins. Spinach was in the very first packets of frozen food sold in Sweden.
howToEat: The tender first leaves are good in salad, and the stalks can be stir-fried or used in soup. The leaves are high in oxalic acid, so don't eat spinach every day.

events.note: Cold-tolerant — sow direct in the cool, bright conservatory.
Late April to May, once the soil has thawed. Spinach bolts in the long June days, so sow early.
Main autumn sowing — shortening days, no bolting.
Leaves from the conservatory sowing.
Pick before it bolts.
Autumn leaves — spinach takes frost.

name: Rocket
description: A fast-growing member of the cabbage family forming low tufts of softly lobed leaves with a mild, peppery, spicy taste. Although linked to Mediterranean food, it grew in Sweden as early as the 1400s.
howToEat: The leaves are best in salad, and can also be made into pesto. Flea beetle holes don't spoil the taste.

events.note: Late April to May — it bolts in the long midsummer days, so sow early or wait for August.
Best sowing — fast, peppery leaves as the days shorten.
Sow in the frost-free conservatory — outdoors there's too little growth left before frost.
Pick young, before it bolts.
Autumn leaves from the August sowing.
Slow winter leaves from the conservatory sowing.

name: Corn salad
description: A very hardy salad plant forming low rosettes of dark green leaves with a unique taste, both green and nutty. It was grown in Sweden as early as the 1600s.
howToEat: Snip leaves or small bunches a little at a time for salad, from late summer until the snow falls and again in early spring.

events.note: Very hardy — sizes up in autumn, sits dormant under snow, then crops again in spring.
Cut whole rosettes until the snow comes.
Overwintered plants crop again once the snow melts, before they flower.

name: Fennel
description: A variety of the herb fennel, grown since ancient Egypt. The 'bulb' is really the swollen base of the stem and has a mild, aniseed-like flavour.
howToEat: Eat the bulb and use the leaves as a herb. Bulbs keep for two to three weeks in the fridge.

events.note: Sow late May in modules — fennel hates root disturbance and bolts if sown before midsummer's long days peak. Pick a bolt-resistant variety.
Plant out late June, module and all.
Cut bulbs at tennis-ball size, before the first frost.

name: Potato
description: A South American tuber that reached Sweden in the 1650s. Farmers once bred hundreds of local varieties, and old heirlooms have a strong taste, more vegetable than potato.
howToEat: Boiled or baked; some varieties stay firm while floury ones fall apart easily. Green potatoes are poisonous and must not be eaten. Store dark and cool. Only the tubers are eaten; the leaves and berries are poisonous.

events.note: Plant chitted earlies early to mid May, once the soil is about 8°C; maincrop after. Earth up if frost threatens.
First earlies ready to dig, from about midsummer to late July.
Second earlies.
Lift maincrop once the tops die back, before the frost. Dry and store dark and cool.

name: Rhubarb
description: A large perennial with long, red or green stalks and huge flower stems up to two metres tall. It contains a lot of oxalic acid, so it's best eaten in moderation.
howToEat: The stalks need sugar when cooked and are classic for jam, cordial and rhubarb pie. Eat the stalks only: the leaves are poisonous, and the stalks are high in oxalic acid, so eat them in moderation (book p. 381).

events.note: First stalks once the ground has thawed — pull, don't cut; twist stems away cleanly.
Peak pulling season. Stop at midsummer so the plant can recover.
Split and replant crowns in spring once the ground has thawed.
Or split in early autumn, so the crowns root before the freeze.

name: Strawberry
notes: Plant in a sunny spot where strawberries have not grown for at least four years, and move the bed every 3-4 years to escape strawberry blossom weevil and soil pests.
Go easy on nitrogen and avoid dense rows to limit grey mould; mulch only once the green fruit starts hanging down.
Cut off runners you don't need, and cover the bed with straw, leaves or fleece over winter.
description: Arrived in Sweden in the 1700s and quickly became a manor-garden favourite. Modern varieties are healthier than the grand old ones, if slightly milder in taste.
howToEat: Eaten fresh straight from the bed; the book also suggests varieties such as Rebecka for hanging baskets and balcony boxes.

events.note: Bought plants can go in once the soil is workable in spring.
The book says plant no later than August; rooted runners are set out in late summer so they establish before winter (book p. 487).
Early, mid and late varieties spread the harvest; expect it 1-2 weeks later in Stockholm than in southern Sweden. Water in the morning and remove damaged berries.

recommendedVarieties.name: Rebecka
recommendedVarieties.ripening: Early; everbearing, first harvest record early

name: Currant
notes: Crops well even in partial shade; feed sparingly, as too much nitrogen invites disease.

Flowers on one-year-old and older shoots, so prune harder than red currants, starting after 3-4 years. Prune at the base in autumn or winter: remove drooping and damaged branches and the 3-4 oldest each year.
Big bud mite makes buds swell like peas and spreads reversion virus; dig up and burn infested bushes.
description: The hardiest of all berry bushes, grown and wild across Sweden; in Tornedalen it is farmed commercially. Variety Polar tolerates spring frost at flowering.

events.note: Plant spring or autumn, as for gooseberry (book p. 497).
Or plant in early autumn so roots establish before the ground freezes. Early October at the latest.
Timing not given in the book; typical mid-late summer harvest in Stockholm.

name: Raspberry
notes: Plant in sun with good drainage in loose, moist soil enriched with compost and manure; dislikes stiff clay. Most varieties need a permanent support.
After harvest cut fruited canes to the ground and thin new canes to about ten per metre; autumn raspberries are simply cut down after harvest.
Buy certified virus-free plants; raspberry beetle, gall midge, cane fly and cane spot are the main problems.
description: Raspberries have been grown in Sweden since the Middle Ages and are part of every classic Swedish garden. They need protection from insects, disease, frost and drought to give good berries.

events.note: Plant at the same depth as in the pot; cut bare-root canes back by a third (book p. 480).
Or plant in early autumn so it roots before the freeze; the book favours August-September (p. 466).
Summer raspberries; the book gives no month, so this is an estimate for Stockholm.
Autumn raspberries ripen from August (book p. 480); the book says they grow only up to zone 3.

name: Apple
notes: Apples need pollen from another variety that flowers at the same time; check E-planta's pollination chart.
Sunny, sheltered spot in well-drained soil, pH about 6-7. On compact clay, plant on a raised bed. Keep the graft knob above ground.
Prune every year for the first ten years. Net young trees against deer and hares, guard the trunk against voles, and give no nitrogen after mid-July.
description: Sweden's most-grown fruit tree. Each tree is a chosen variety grafted onto a rootstock that decides its size and hardiness; the common A2 rootstock gives a large, hardy tree. Hardy varieties for zone 3 include Silva (zone 1-6), Oranie and Gyllenkroks Astrakan (1-5).
howToEat: Eat fresh, or cook into apple sauce, pies and juice. Winter apples store through the winter somewhere cool.

name: Plum
notes: Many plums are self-fertile, e.g. Victoria, Opal, Herman and Reine Claude d'Oullins, so one tree can crop alone.
Sunny, sheltered spot in well-drained soil, pH about 6-7. Don't plant where a plum or cherry grew before; an apple spot is fine.
Hardiest varieties: Tunaplommon (zone 1-5) and Opal (1-4).
description: A stone fruit tree, grafted like apples. Swedish hardy varieties include old local types such as Tunaplommon from Medelpad, a small, sweet, yellow plum that grows up to zone 5.
howToEat: Eat fresh, or make jam and compote. Prune-type varieties can be dried.

name: Earthnut pea
notes: Very easy to grow but can spread and become a weed.
Yield of the small chestnut-flavoured tubers is modest; store them like potatoes.
description: A perennial, metre-tall pea plant with fragrant purple-red flowers and black tubers 4–5 cm long that look eerily like mice, tail and all. 19th-century royalty prized their chestnut-like flavour.
howToEat: Dig the tubers in autumn and store them like potatoes. The yield is very modest.

events.note: Plant tubers 5 cm deep early in spring, once the soil is workable (book p. 256).
Dig tubers in autumn; leaving them in the ground over winter risks losses (book p. 256).

name: Soybean
notes: Short-day plant: pods form late and may not ripen outside southern Sweden.
Grow in light, humus-rich soil in a sunny, sheltered spot; Fiskeby V works in Sweden.
Dry harvested pods indoors for a couple of weeks before shelling, or eat young green beans cooked.
description: A protein-rich bean that only forms pods late in summer as the days get shorter, so it is tricky to ripen outside southern Sweden.
howToEat: Let the beans dry indoors for a couple of weeks before shelling them, or pick them green and eat them fresh after boiling. Always cook soybeans; raw beans are poisonous.

events.note: Start indoors; the book says starting indoors is the safest method (book p. 256).
Plant out after the frost risk has passed (book p. 256).
Harvest as late as possible so beans mature, but before the late-September frosts.

name: Asparagus pea
notes: Needs moist, humus-rich soil and a sunny spot.
Pick pods at about 3 cm long, otherwise they turn tough; crops for up to two months.
description: A low, 20 cm plant with dark purple flowers and exotic square, winged pods. It came to Sweden in the 1800s and was one of the trendiest vegetables for a few decades before being forgotten.
howToEat: Pick the pods when they are about 3 cm long, when they taste delicate. Boil them only lightly and enjoy them with butter.

events.note: Sow indoors early in spring (book p. 256).
Plant out from late May, 10 cm apart, under fleece at first.
Or sow direct once the soil is 10-12 °C and cover with fleece (book p. 256).
Pick pods young, about 3 cm long (book p. 256).

name: Chinese broccoli
notes: Sow in late summer: spring and early-summer sowings bolt quickly (book p. 261).
Late-summer sowings give more compact plants; eat stems, flower buds and leaves.
Flea beetles and caterpillars attack; cover with fleece without gaps.
description: Also called kai-lan or Chinese broccoli, it doesn't look like ordinary broccoli: a 40 cm plant with thick stems and small white flowers that don't form a head. The flavour is excellent.
howToEat: Eat all parts: stems, flower buds and leaves, cut when the first bud opens. Use like other Asian greens, but only young stems and shoots are good in salad.

events.note: Sow direct in late summer only; the book advises skipping spring and early-summer sowings (book p. 260).
Cut the main shoot when the first flower bud opens, then side shoots (book p. 262).

name: Chinese cabbage
notes: The book recommends the open-headed type: richer flavour and faster growth than hearting types.
Blanch inner leaves by slipping a rubber band over the top a couple of weeks before harvest.
Flea beetles are the worst pest; dust leaves with ash or rock dust and cover with fleece without gaps.
description: Chinese cabbage, sold cheaply in every supermarket, is actually Asian. The open-hearted type, whose head doesn't close, has a richer flavour and grows faster.
howToEat: Use raw in salads, in soups, stir-fried or in pies like other Asian greens. Blanching the plant under a rubber band for a couple of weeks before harvest makes the inner leaves more tender.

events.note: Sow direct in rounds every two weeks, July to mid-August for Stockholm (book p. 262).
Cut a few cm above ground for regrowth; harvest at once if it starts to flower (book p. 262).

name: Tatsoi
notes: Flat rosette 30-40 cm across; stems are coarser, so cook rather than use in salads.
Survives -8 °C and a little frost improves the flavour.
Flea beetles are the worst pest; dust leaves with ash or rock dust and cover with fleece without gaps.
description: A striking Asian green with a head as flat as a pancake and leaves arranged in a neat rosette. It tastes like pak choi, and a light frost even improves the flavour.
howToEat: Eat both leaves and stems, cooked or stir-fried. They are a bit coarse, so not suited to salad.

events.note: Sow direct in rounds every two weeks, July to mid-August for Stockholm (book p. 262).
Very frost-hardy, so harvest into late autumn (book p. 261).

name: Chicory
notes: Covers radicchio (rosensallat), sugarloaf (sallatscikoria) and witloof for forcing; hardier than lettuce.
Grow like lettuce but sow a couple of weeks later, as cool soil causes bolting; give liquid feed in summer.
Radicchio and sugarloaf heads often only form when autumn cold arrives.
description: Descended from the sky-blue wild chicory flower, this group includes radicchio, sugarloaf and forced Belgian endive. The leaves have a piquant, bitter taste, and the plants are hardier than ordinary lettuce.
howToEat: Mix the bitter leaves with milder lettuce in salads. Forced roots give crisp white endive by Christmas, and Treviso-type radicchio is also used in cooking. Keeps longer than lettuce.

imageCredit.author: The original uploader was Kasteelhoeve Puth at English Wikipedia.

foraging.picking: Looks like dandelion when young, but the pale blue flowers make it obvious. Often lines roadside ditches. Rock the root up by gripping the stem base while digging gently.
foraging.habitat: Cultivated land and along roads; likes dry sites.
foraging.identification: Stiff stem, pinnately lobed lower leaves, branching towards the top, strap-shaped flowers.

lookAlikes.name: Dandelion
lookAlikes.howToTell: Easily confused before flowering; chicory is slightly hairy on the leaf undersides.

events.note: Starting indoors gives earlier harvest and bigger heads (book p. 264).
Plant out 20-30 cm apart once the soil is warm.
Or sow direct, a couple of weeks after lettuce, when soil reaches 12 °C (book p. 264).
Do not rush radicchio and sugarloaf; lift witloof roots for forcing in late autumn (book p. 264).
Force witloof roots in a dark place at 15-20 °C for blanched chicons by Christmas (book p. 264).

name: Endive
notes: Covers frisée and escarole; shortest development time of the chicories.
Blanch 7-10 days before harvest with a clothes peg, rubber band or bucket to soften bitterness.
Slugs and aphids are the only usual pests.
description: A chicory forming huge rosettes of curly, deeply cut leaves. They can be a bit too bitter, but self-blanching varieties are now available.
howToEat: Blanch the head for a week or so before harvest to make the flavour milder, then use it in salads. It keeps longer than ordinary lettuce.

events.note: Sow direct, a couple of weeks later than lettuce, when soil reaches 12 °C (book p. 264).
Harvest before plants bolt, after blanching for 7-10 days (book p. 266).

name: Dill
notes: Needs loose, fertile, moist soil; never let it dry out, so mulch.
High phosphorus need: bone meal helps; red or blue-green leaves signal shortage.
Rotate every four years to avoid damping-off and fungal disease; fleece keeps aphids off.
description: A herb from Asia grown by the Egyptians, Greeks and Romans. It thrives in Sweden's cool climate and is said to taste even better here than in southern heat.
howToEat: Pick the leaves as needed before flowering. The flower heads (crown dill) are cut as flowering ends, and seeds can be collected once dry and brown.

events.note: Sow leaf dill direct in three or four rounds from late April (book p. 267).
Pick leaves before flowering; cut dill crowns as flowering ends (book p. 267).

name: New Zealand spinach
notes: Soak seeds for a day to speed slow germination.
Wants rich, loose soil; give liquid feed a couple of times in summer and water for best growth.
Pinch tips regularly to encourage new shoots; slugs are the main pest.
description: A lush, sprawling plant with thick, juicy leaves, brought to Europe from New Zealand by a British explorer in the 1700s. Its flavour is not as round as true spinach.
howToEat: Use it as a summer substitute for ordinary spinach. Surplus leaves can be frozen the same way as spinach.

events.note: Start indoors 4-5 weeks before planting out (book p. 270).
Plant out after 20 May; does not tolerate frost.
Pinch off a few leaves per plant; stop at the first frost (book p. 270).

name: Parsley
notes: Soak seeds in lukewarm water overnight to speed slow germination.
Give liquid feed a few times in summer and water in drought.
Fleece from sowing to harvest protects against carrot fly larvae.
description: Grown around the Mediterranean since ancient times and in Sweden since the 1700s. Curly parsley was long the favourite, but the more flavourful flat-leaf type is catching up. Both are very rich in vitamin A.
howToEat: Parsley is best fresh. For freezing, choose flat-leaf parsley, which keeps its flavour better.

events.note: Optionally start a few plants indoors in March or April for an earlier harvest (book p. 271).
Plant out hardy seedlings in May.
Sow direct from late April; germination is slow (book p. 271).
Pick leaves as needed far into late autumn (book p. 271).

name: Water spinach
notes: Needs 24 °C or more and dies below 10 °C, so grow under glass, plastic or fleece.
Use fresh seed soaked overnight; it loses viability after two years.
Water daily and mulch with fresh grass clippings for moisture and nitrogen.
description: A heat-loving Southeast Asian leaf vegetable, often grown in running water and so also called water spinach. Its green leaves and crisp, hollow stems taste sweet and mild like spinach, with more bite.
howToEat: Use like ordinary spinach, but in China it is above all a stir-fry vegetable. Cut the stems into pieces and stir-fry them a minute or two longer than the leaves.

events.note: Start indoors, preferably early May, at 20-22 °C (book p. 276).
Plant out when the soil is warm and frost is over; it needs glass or plastic cover (book p. 276).
Cut shoots as needed, leaving at least 5 cm of stem (book p. 275).

name: Wild rocket
notes: Slower than rocket but slower to bolt; crops most of the summer.
Needs loose soil that never dries out, in sun or light shade.
Cover with dry leaves or straw in winter to improve overwintering.
description: Also called wild rocket, this perennial forms low rosettes of lobed leaves that taste like rocket but a bit sharper. It grows wild in southern Sweden.
howToEat: Pick the leaves at the base as needed. The flowers are edible too.

events.note: For a head start, sow indoors a month before planting out (book p. 277).
Plant out after the frost risk is over (book p. 277).
Or sow direct once the soil is warm; barely cover the tiny seeds (book p. 277).
Pick leaves at the base as needed; established plants crop from spring (book p. 278).

name: Garden cress
notes: Fast and shallow-rooted: sow between slow crops or in boxes and troughs.
Pause sowing in high summer when it bolts fast, or sow in partial shade.
Large-leaved varieties are best for growing outdoors.
description: The kitchen garden's sprinter: a fast-growing cress with spicy, more or less curly leaves. Grown outdoors in beds, as in the Middle East, it forms generous bunches, and large-leaved types are now available.
howToEat: Snip the spicy leaves and stems into salads or onto sandwiches. The flowers are edible too.

events.note: Sow direct in small rounds from late April; skip high summer (book p. 278).
Cut as soon as there are leaves; pull the whole plant if it flowers (book p. 278).

name: Celery
notes: Easier and faster than celeriac or celery; good in pots.
Needs moist, loose soil and must not dry out; liquid feed in high and late summer.
Cut back to 2 cm in late summer if the plant looks coarse to get fresh leaves.
description: A little-known relative of celeriac and celery, grown for its leaves, which have a strong celery taste and smell. It forms bushy plants with thin stalks and is one of the most important vegetables in Asia.
howToEat: Use as a herb or in soups and stews. In Asia leaves and stalks are stir-fried with meat or dried for soup. Add only a few young leaves to salad, or everything tastes of celery.

events.note: Start indoors; tiny seeds need light to germinate, so barely cover them (book p. 279).
Plant out once it stays above 12 °C, or it may bolt (book p. 279).
Cut stems at the base regularly until winter (book p. 280).

name: Purslane
notes: Needs a sunny spot and warm, humus-rich, moist soil; cover sowings with fleece until established.
In wet summers slugs are a big problem: skip mulch and pick slugs daily.
description: A sun-loving plant with sour, slightly succulent leaves. Green types taste sharper and finer, while yellow ones are prettier but milder. The leaves are rich in omega-3 fatty acids and vitamin E.
howToEat: The leaves and tender stems are refreshing in a mixed salad, or just eaten straight from the plant on a hot day.

events.note: In a harsh climate always start indoors, from late April (book p. 283).
Plant out after 20 May once the weather is warm.
Or sow direct when soil reaches 12 °C, at bean-sowing time (book p. 282).
Harvest leaves and young stems from July, leaving a few basal leaves (book p. 283).

name: Strawberry spinach
notes: Barely cover the seed, as it germinates best with some light; fleece helps the slow start.
Keep the soil moist; like other goosefoots it dislikes drought.
Both the red berries and the leaves are edible; use leaves like spinach.
description: A curiosity grown mostly for its looks, with red berries scattered along the stems like wild strawberries threaded on a straw. It was already described as a curiosity in a French garden book from 1885.
howToEat: The berries are edible, though not as tasty as strawberries. The leaves are used like spinach.

events.note: Sow direct in a sunny spot once the soil is warm, under fleece at first (book p. 285).
Plants get going from mid July; pick leaves here and there (book p. 285).

name: Good King Henry
notes: Hardy perennial forming 50-80 cm clumps; needs rich, loose, moist soil.
Young spring shoots can be blanched and eaten like asparagus; leaves used like spinach all summer.
description: A hardy perennial that forms large clumps and is often found at old crofts. Not a culinary highlight, but a great survivor: it was grown as early as the 1100s.
howToEat: The leaves were once used like spinach all summer. The young spring shoots were blanched and eaten like asparagus.

events.note: For just a few plants, sow in pots indoors and plant out later (book p. 285).
Plant out 30 cm apart in rich, moist soil (book p. 285).
Pick young shoots in spring and leaves all summer (book p. 285).

name: Ice plant
notes: Grow in loose, well-drained soil, preferably under fleece.
Succulent, salty leaves are best raw in salads; they go limp when cooked.
description: A plant with thick, juicy leaves covered in what looks like ice crystals that glitter in the sun. The taste is sour and slightly salty.
howToEat: Best raw in salad. Some cook the leaves like spinach, but they lose their crunch and turn limp.

events.note: Seeds are small, so start indoors; they germinate well at room temperature (book p. 286).
Plant out after 20 May under fleece; grown like summer purslane (book p. 286).
Pick leaves as needed until late September.

name: Mallow
notes: Grow in moist, rich soil; mulch with grass clippings or liquid-feed in summer.
Leaves are only good in early summer and summer, then turn coarse. Often self-seeds.
description: To most people a summer flower, but in southern Europe and much of Asia also a leaf vegetable. Whorled mallow is used around the Mediterranean, and a curly-edged form in East Asia.
howToEat: Use the leaves in salad or like spinach, picked in early summer and summer before they turn tough.

events.note: Sow direct and thin to 20 cm (book p. 286).
Harvest leaves in early summer and summer only (book p. 286).

name: Milk thistle
notes: Needs sun and deep, rich soil; copes with heavy clay.
Very spiny: wear gloves. Light boiling softens the spines; use leaves like spinach.
Biennial grown as an annual, about 1 m tall.
description: A striking plant with huge silver-grey leaves and needle-sharp spines, grown mostly as an ornamental. In southern Europe it has at times been used in the kitchen as a spinach.
howToEat: Lightly boil the leaves like spinach, which makes the spines harmless. Wear gloves when picking.

events.note: Start indoors (book p. 286).
Plant out into warm soil in full sun after 20 May (book p. 286).
Cut leaves or whole rosettes as needed (book p. 286).

name: Mitsuba
notes: Prefers part shade; never let the soil dry out and liquid-feed a couple of times.
Cut shoots continually like parsley; if leaves get coarse, cut all at the base for regrowth.
description: A Japanese leaf vegetable that looks like flat-leaf parsley but tastes different, slightly wild. It is perennial and often survives the winter in southern and central Sweden.
howToEat: Use the leaves in stir-fries, ideally with fish or chicken. A few leaves give fish soup a richer flavour.

events.note: Start indoors in March or April (book p. 286-287).
Plant out once the soil is warm, ideally in part shade (book p. 287).
Cut shoots continually, as with parsley (book p. 287).

name: Quinoa
notes: Sow in full sun in deep, rich soil; plants grow over 1 m tall.
Leaves are plentiful and used like spinach; seed yield is modest in a cool summer.
description: Grown in South America for nearly 5,000 years, for both leaves and very nutritious seeds that hold twice as much protein as wheat. In Sweden the seed harvest is modest, but leaves come in plenty.
howToEat: The leaves taste like spinach and are used the same way. The seeds go into salads, smoothies and baking. Rinse the seeds well before cooking to wash off their bitter coating.

events.note: Sow direct in full sun (book p. 287).
Pick leaves through summer; harvest seeds when golden yellow (book p. 287).

name: Amaranth
notes: Heat-loving: sow only into warm soil and cover the tiny seeds very thinly.
Liquid-feed regularly, as the leaves use a lot of nitrogen.
description: Also called Chinese spinach, it gives lots of spinach-like leaves with a slightly bittersweet taste, full of minerals and vitamins. Most varieties are strikingly beautiful, in dark wine red and green.
howToEat: Use the leaves like spinach. In Asia they are stir-fried, often with a little mint and garlic.

events.note: Optionally start plants indoors (book p. 287).
Book says sow direct late May/early June in warm soil; shifted to June for Stockholm, under fleece (book p. 287).
Plant out indoor-raised plants once nights are warm.
Start at about 15 cm tall, then pinch shoots as needed (book p. 287).

name: Salad burnet
notes: Sunny or lightly shaded spot with loose, rich, moisture-retentive soil.
Cut leaves regularly for new growth; harvest ends when leaves turn bitter and coarse.
description: A wild perennial herb with graceful rosettes of saw-toothed leaves and a cucumber-like, slightly tart taste. In the 1700s it was both a vegetable and a flavouring for schnapps and red wine.
howToEat: Add the leaves to a mixed salad to round out the flavour. Pick regularly; older leaves turn bitter and tough.

events.note: Sow once the soil is warm, cover very thinly; germination takes about two weeks (book p. 288).
Cut leaves regularly (book p. 288).

name: Caucasian spinach
notes: Vigorous perennial climber reaching 3-4 m; give it a sturdy support and deep, rich soil.
Seeds need a cold treatment; divide the plant after a few years.
description: A vigorous perennial climber from the Caucasus that can reach several metres in a season. It is the first green to appear in spring and came to Sweden in the 1860s.
howToEat: Use the leaves like spinach in spring and early summer. The rest of the year the plant is ornamental.

events.note: Sow in moist pots and chill in the fridge for 1-2 weeks first; usually only a few seeds germinate (book p. 288).
Plant out by a sturdy climbing support.
Leaves are among the first up; use as spinach in spring and early summer (book p. 288).

name: Garland chrysanthemum
notes: Thrives in part shade; moist soil prevents bolting in summer heat.
Leaves become inedible once it flowers, but the flowers are edible.
description: The same species as the annual crown daisy, bred in China and Japan into a leaf vegetable with a fresh, fruity taste. Also known as shungiku.
howToEat: Stir-fry the leaves or cook like spinach; the youngest leaves can be eaten raw in salad. Leaves are inedible once it flowers, but the flowers make a garnish or tea.

events.note: Sow direct in rounds; ready in about 40 days (book p. 289).
Start picking at 10-15 cm tall (book p. 289).

name: Sorrel
notes: Loose soil is essential; keep weeded and moist, as drought spoils the flavour.
Cut off flower stems to prolong harvest; feed lightly in spring.
Rejuvenate after a few years by dividing in spring.
description: A low, ground-covering sorrel with pretty grey-green, shield-shaped leaves on thin stalks. It is mildly sour and a favourite of French gourmet chefs, who rate its flavour above common sorrel.
howToEat: Use it the same way as garden sorrel: mixed with spinach, or in fish soup or fish sauce.

events.note: Start indoors in April (book p. 289).
Plant out after the frost risk, from 20 May, in sun or part shade (book p. 289).
Pick leaves as needed.

name: Agretti
notes: Seed is expensive and often germinates poorly, so start indoors.
Needs a sunny spot and loose soil; harvest top shoots continually.
description: A seaside plant with salty, crunchy, chive-like leaves that tangle into a green mat, known in Italy as agretti and prized by Italian chefs.
howToEat: Tastiest raw in a mixed salad. It can also be sautéed in olive oil and served with pasta, fish or seafood. In Japan it is eaten with sushi.

events.note: Author starts indoors at the end of March; shifted to early April for Stockholm (book p. 289).
Book plants out in May; after 20 May for Stockholm (book p. 291).
Book starts harvest late June and picks until frost (book p. 291).

name: Lettuce
notes: Grown like head lettuce but needs a longer season; mainly grown for the thick stem.
Take only a few lower leaves, or stem growth is checked.
description: A lettuce grown mainly for its thick, juicy stem, widely grown in China. Its leaves are a little coarser than ordinary head lettuce.
howToEat: Eat the stem boiled, or raw like cucumber. The lower leaves can be eaten too, but don't take too many.

events.note: Grown like head lettuce; start indoors for the longer season (book p. 291).
Plant out 35 cm apart (book p. 291).
Cut the stem at about 30 cm tall and 2.5 cm thick (book p. 291).

name: Patience dock
notes: Sun or part shade in moist, rich soil; cut flower spikes or leaves stop growing.
Liquid-feed for repeat harvests; divide and move every 3-4 years.
description: A faithful perennial dock, thought to have been introduced by monks. It is related to garden sorrel but is less sour.
howToEat: Eat the leaves like spinach. They are tastiest in spring.

events.note: Seedlings should be started indoors, or buy plants (book p. 291).
Plant out 40-50 cm apart (book p. 291).
Leaves are best in spring; use as spinach (book p. 291).

name: Orach
notes: Top the plant continually and keep feeding for fresh leaves all summer.
Leaves are unusable once it flowers; plants reach 2 m.
description: In the Middle Ages this was the spinach, and finds in Lund show it was grown in the 1100s. A relative of fat hen with much larger leaves, it can grow two metres tall. Red-leaved forms look stunning.
howToEat: Use the leaves like spinach; they are best young and tender. Green-leaved orach tastes better than red. Once it flowers, the leaves are no longer usable.

events.note: Sow direct early in spring, from late April (book p. 291).
Start picking young leaves at 7-8 leaves (book p. 291).

name: Sorrel
notes: Hardy perennial that returns with little care; grown like patience dock.
Very sour: mix half and half with spinach, or use in fish soups and sauces.
description: A hardy perennial whose leaves taste like wild meadow sorrel. It was grown in Sweden in the 1600s, then almost disappeared.
howToEat: Used on its own like spinach it is rather sharp, so mix half sorrel with half spinach. The leaves are also good in fish soup or fish sauce.

events.note: Grown like patience dock: start indoors (book p. 292).
Plant out in sun or part shade in moist, rich soil.
Pick leaves as needed.

name: Watercress
notes: Grow under plastic or fleece in very porous soil and water daily.
Pinch off flower stems, leave a third of shoots, and liquid-feed a couple of times.
description: A perennial that grows wild in much of the world, including a few streams in Skåne. It was traditionally grown in running water.

events.note: Sow direct under fleece or in a tunnel, thin to 5 cm (book p. 292).
Cut stems and leaves; growth is strongest in late autumn (book p. 292-293).

name: Winter purslane
notes: Easy, cold-tolerant plant grown like corn salad in sun or light shade.
Sow a second round in late summer for leaves into late autumn.
description: A hardy, easy plant with round, fleshy leaves and a fresh, slightly sour taste.
howToEat: Use the leaves fresh in salad.

events.note: Sow as soon as the soil is workable, from late April (book p. 293).
Sow a late-summer round for leaves into late autumn (book p. 293).
Pick leaves as needed for fresh salads (book p. 293).

name: Land cress
notes: Easy but modest yield; wants sun, tolerates some shade.
Cover seed very thinly and keep the sowing moist.
description: Also called winter cress, as its leaves taste almost like watercress and are very cold-hardy. It forms a dense rosette of dark green, glossy, rounded leaves. It was grown in the 1600s, then forgotten.
howToEat: The strong-tasting leaves work well in both salad and soup.

events.note: Sow once the soil is workable, from late April, or in rounds (book p. 293).
Very cold-tolerant: pick leaves far into autumn (book p. 293).

name: Melon
notes: Grow in the greenhouse in very rich, warm, compost-heavy soil; pinch side shoots after three to five leaves.
Hand-pollinate in the morning with a brush; ventilate above 30 °C and mulch with grass clippings.
Ripe when the colour turns, the stalk end softens and the fruit smells of melon.
description: A close relative of the cucumber that needs even more warmth, grown for pleasure rather than a big harvest. Honeydew melons have sweet, aromatic flesh, and small watermelons can also be grown here.
howToEat: Eat fresh once ripe: the fruit has its proper colour, comes away easily, is soft around the stalk and smells of melon.

imageCredit.author: USDA photo by Scott Bauer. Image Number K7355-11.

events.note: Always start indoors; needs warmth to germinate (book p. 301).
Move into the greenhouse from late May once nights stay frost-free.
Pick when the fruit slips easily from the stalk and smells sweet.

name: Broccoli raab
notes: Needs loose, well-manured soil and steady watering; thin early or plants bolt.
Skip midsummer sowings, which bolt; the late-July sowing often does best.
Choose early varieties such as Quarantina; they beat the caterpillars.
description: A fast-growing annual cabbage relative that looks like a small broccoli with more delicate leaves and a hint of bitterness. Its strong taste is somewhere between mustard greens and broccoli; in Italy it's called cima di rape.
howToEat: Italians use the young shoots and flower heads in pasta sauces, soups and stews. Cut the shoots into short pieces and fry them with garlic and a little olive oil for two minutes.

events.note: Sow direct once the soil is warm, about 15 °C (book p. 310).
Second sowing mid-July, then liquid-feed; mid to late July in the book (book p. 310).
Cut shoots while still in bud, repeatedly, until the plant bolts.

name: Broccoli
notes: Grow like broccoli but sow a couple of weeks later, as heads go loose in midsummer heat.
Never let it dry out; cover with fleece against caterpillars and cabbage root fly.
Lower yield and longer season than broccoli; Romanesco Natalino is the book's pick.
description: A cross between cauliflower and broccoli with a yellow-green, pagoda-shaped head. It gives a smaller harvest than broccoli and takes longer to mature.

events.note: Start indoors 4-6 weeks before planting out, then grow on cool (book p. 318). Sow a couple of weeks later than broccoli (book p. 307).
Plant out hardened plants in late May, slightly deeper than in the pot, under fleece.
Cut heads when tight and fully formed.

name: Brussels sprouts
notes: Long season and fussy: avoid very light soil and always start indoors.
Keep weeding and hoeing into autumn; fleece against caterpillars and root fly.
Flavour improves after a few frosts; blanch and freeze to store.
description: The youngest cabbage type, which appeared around Brussels in the 1400s. Tiny cabbage-like heads about 3 cm across grow up a tall stem, in green or red varieties.
howToEat: The flavour gets better after a few frosty nights. The best way to keep the sprouts is to blanch and freeze them.

events.note: Start indoors 4-6 weeks before planting out, then grow on cool (book p. 318). Sow early April; the season is long (book p. 311).
Plant out hardened plants in late May, slightly deeper than in the pot, under fleece.
Pick sprouts from the bottom up as they firm, after the first frosts.

name: Kale
notes: As easy as kale and frost tolerant, though not quite as hardy.
Use the widest spacing for a statuesque plant, closer for more leaves to eat.
Start picking outer leaves at eight to ten leaves; do not strip too many at once.
description: An old Italian kale with an elegant, palm-like shape and unique blue-black, bubbly leaves like savoy cabbage. It was grown in Sweden in the 1800s and is so handsome it is grown as an ornamental.
howToEat: Use the leaves like chard, Italian-style with olive oil, shallot and lemon; Italians love them most in soup. Some smaller varieties are used as baby leaves in salad.

events.note: Start indoors 4-6 weeks before planting out, then grow on cool (book p. 318).
Plant out hardened plants in late May, slightly deeper than in the pot, under fleece.
Pick outer leaves as needed; lift the whole plant in late autumn.

name: Cabbage
notes: Easier than white cabbage and grown the same way; rich, moist soil and regular feeding.
Fleece from planting out against caterpillars, flea beetles and cabbage root fly.
Early types split if left; late types are hardier but do not store, so eat in autumn.
description: Looks like white cabbage but has grey-green, crinkled outer leaves and a loose head that is yellow, crisp and mild inside. The author thinks it tastes better than white cabbage; the name may come from Savoy in northern Italy.
howToEat: Savoy cabbage can't be stored, so eat it during the autumn.

events.note: Start indoors 4-6 weeks before planting out, then grow on cool (book p. 318).
Plant out hardened plants in late May, slightly deeper than in the pot, under fleece.
Cut early types as soon as heads are ready; late types into October.

name: Siberian kale
notes: Fast, mild and cold-hardy; sweeter after frost and good raw in salads.
Full sun is best but tolerates part shade; thin for big plants.
Same pests as other brassicas but suffers less.
description: A leafy kale relative, probably a natural cross between kale and rapeseed from northern Asia. It is crisper and milder than ordinary kale, so children like it more, and comes in grey shades with red or white leaf veins.
howToEat: Great in salad. Use small leaves raw in salad and large leaves for cooking. It gets even tastier after frost.

events.note: Easiest sown direct from late April; can also be started indoors (book p. 317).
Pick outer leaves in rounds: small for salad, large for cooking.

name: Cabbage
notes: Fleece is essential: caterpillars and slugs love the tender yellow leaves.
Otherwise grow like white cabbage in rich, moist soil.
Eat fresh in salad; it does not store.
description: A traditional German cabbage that looks like a cross between pointed cabbage and savoy, with pale yellow leaves in a loose head. It gets its name from its wonderfully buttery taste.
howToEat: Eat it fresh in salad, or possibly cooked in butter; the author says anything else is a waste.

events.note: Start indoors 4-6 weeks before planting out, then grow on cool (book p. 318).
Plant out hardened plants in late May, slightly deeper than in the pot, under fleece.
Pick leaves once the head starts closing about three months after sowing, or cut the whole head in late autumn.

name: Cabbage
notes: Slower than white cabbage, especially at first; rich humus clay soil gives the best heads.
Feed every two weeks or mulch with grass clippings; fleece against caterpillars and root fly.
Rotate strictly because of clubroot; store heads cool, near 0 °C.
description: Simply a red-leaved form of white cabbage. It grows more slowly and its heads are a little smaller; the red pointed variety Kalibos is a favourite of the author for its tenderness and flavour.

events.note: Start indoors 4-6 weeks before planting out, then grow on cool (book p. 318).
Plant out hardened plants in late May, slightly deeper than in the pot, under fleece.
Cut when heads are full and firm, before they split; early types from August.

name: Chives
notes: Easiest started from a divided clump; likes loose, moist soil in sun or part shade.
Cut the whole clump two or three times a season for fresh leaves and fewer flowers.
Divide, move and feed every three to four years.
description: A hardy perennial forming clumps of hollow, grass-like leaves with dark pink flower balls. It has been grown in Europe since the 1500s, and Dutch farmers are said to have fed it to cows so the milk tasted of chives.
howToEat: Snip the leaves as needed; cutting back keeps new tender leaves coming, as flowering makes them inedible. Extra chives can be cut into small pieces and frozen.

events.note: Start indoors in April, about fifty seeds per pot for a full clump (book p. 324).
Plant out the seedling clumps once the soil has warmed (book p. 324).
Cut as needed; freeze surplus chopped.
Plant bought plants or divisions; divide clumps in spring or autumn (book p. 324).
Cut as needed; freeze surplus chopped.

name: Shallot
notes: Always grown from sets; about 2 cm sets give the best-sized bulbs.
Needs sun, humus-rich loose soil and even watering; weed early, onions hate competition.
Fleece at planting against onion fly; dry bulbs before storing.
description: An easy relative of the onion that forms a cluster of four to eight small bulbs. It has a mild flavour and doesn't bring floods of tears when chopped, which makes it a favourite with chefs.
howToEat: Use it like a mild onion. Dry and store it like ordinary onions.

events.note: Plant sets as soon as the soil is workable, a quarter of the bulb showing (book p. 326).
Lift when just over half the foliage has fallen; dry before storing.

name: Onion
notes: Stays put for years, so give it well-manured soil and full sun.
Sterile: plant aerial bulbils about 5 cm deep, ideally in clusters, and divide every three to four years.
Rarely troubled by pests or disease; store bulbils dry and frost-free.
description: A hardy perennial onion that grows funny little bulbs at the top of its hollow stems, sometimes in two tiers, which makes it a hit with children. Probably a natural hybrid of onion and Welsh onion, first mentioned in 1587.
howToEat: The small top bulbs are lovely in soup and keep dry and frost-free. Pinch off single leaves to use like spring onion; the underground bulb can be used like an ordinary onion.

events.note: Plant bulbils spring or autumn (book p. 329).
Pick the top bulbils before they drop; snip leaves as spring onions anytime.

name: Welsh onion
notes: Very hardy clump-forming onion, most useful in spring before other onions.
Keep weeds out of the clumps, water in drought and earth up stems to blanch them.
Lift, divide and replant every three to four years.
description: A very hardy perennial onion from Siberia forming clumps of thick, hollow stems with white flowers that attract bees. It was common in old Swedish kitchen gardens, often called winter onion.
howToEat: Especially welcome in spring, when no other onion is available. Earthed-up stems turn white and tender.

events.note: Start indoors in March or April, about ten seeds per pot (book p. 331).
Plant out clumps when the soil is warm, cutting the leaves back to 5-6 cm first.
Ease out stems one at a time; a few degrees of frost is no problem.

name: Garlic chives
notes: Wants loose, rich soil and water when dry; garlic-flavoured leaves, buds and flower stalks are all eaten.
Pick leaves continually to keep new growth coming; clumps can be divided.
Perennial but only reliably hardy in southern Sweden, so treat as annual if it fails.
description: A perennial with flat leaves and large white flower heads, grown in China for over 3,000 years. The leaves taste of garlic.
howToEat: Eat the garlic-flavoured leaves; the flower stalks and flower buds are also delicious.

events.note: Start indoors February to March, about ten seeds per pot (book p. 336).
Plant out when the soil is warm, ideally under fleece.
Cut leaves continuously.

name: Norrland onion
notes: Extremely hardy perennial leaf onion that returns every year.
Prized for juicy early spring leaves; snip and freeze surplus for winter.
Hard to find; look for plants from small nurseries.
description: A mysterious, extremely hardy perennial leaf onion found in old gardens, mainly in northern Sweden. It grows 50-60 cm tall with broad stems and pink flowers in summer.
howToEat: Prized for its juicy leaves that come early in spring. Snip them into a bag and freeze them for use through the winter.

events.note: Plant bought plants in spring.
Cut leaves from early spring; freeze surplus.

name: Shallot
notes: Grown exactly like shallot; hardier and stores better.
Never replant bulbs from plants that bolted.
Store dry over winter.
description: A Nordic, more primitive form of shallot, so close that even experts can't tell them apart. Its cloves are usually flatter, hardier and keep better than shallots.
howToEat: Store the bulbs dry over winter; they keep better than shallots.

events.note: Plant sets as soon as the soil is workable, as for shallot (book p. 338).
Lift when over half the foliage has fallen; dry well.

name: Wild garlic
notes: Grows in shade, e.g. under berry bushes, in moist humus-rich soil; dig in compost, no other feed.
Leaves appear early in spring; the plant dies back in midsummer.
Easy to divide.
description: A perennial that grows wild on Gotland, forming onion-scented carpets covered in snow-white flowers in May. It was grown at Vadstena monastery.
howToEat: Use the early spring leaves like chives; they have a faint garlic taste.

foraging.picking: Leaves, flowers, buds and seed capsules are all good to pick. Be sparing, as it grows in few places, and check local rules since it is protected in some counties.
foraging.identification: Garlic smell; grows in large clumps with large smooth leaves; white flowers in rounded umbel-like clusters.

lookAlikes.name: Lily of the valley
lookAlikes.howToTell: Its leaves are rougher and more waxy and do not smell of garlic; the flowers look clearly different.

foraging.safety: Lily of the valley is poisonous and looks very similar to an untrained eye. Pick sparingly; protected in some counties.

events.note: Start seed in pots rather than direct (book p. 338).
Plant out pot-grown plants 15–20 cm apart in shade (book p. 338).
Pick leaves in spring before it dies down.
Plant divisions 15–20 cm apart in shade (book p. 338).
Pick leaves in spring before it dies down.

name: Sand leek
notes: Likes full sun and loose soil.
Divide every other year and feed at the same time.
Leaves, the black bulbils in the flower heads and the garlic-like bulb are all edible.
description: A perennial that looks like a thin leek, with onion-flavoured leaves and violet flower heads holding black bulbils. It grows wild on Gotland, where it was used for soups in the 1700s.
howToEat: Use the leaves in soup, as Gotlanders still sometimes do. The black bulbils can be eaten, and the garlic-like underground bulb is edible too.

events.note: Easy to sow, 15 x 15 cm (book p. 338).
Pick leaves in early summer, bulbils in July-August.
Plant bulbils or divisions; divide every other year.
Pick leaves in early summer, bulbils in July-August.

name: Jerusalem artichoke
notes: Grows almost anywhere if drained; best yield in light, deep, rich soil. Replant in a new spot each year.
Mulch with grass clippings for food and even moisture, especially in late summer when tubers swell.
Lift every small tuber or it becomes a weed; tubers keep best left in the ground.
description: A tall perennial relative of the sunflower with knobbly, fist-sized tubers that taste like globe artichoke. It came from North America in the 1600s and was forgotten once potatoes arrived.
howToEat: Best boiled and served with butter. Tubers dug in spring are even tastier and don't fall apart as easily when cooked.

events.note: Plant tubers 10-15 cm deep once the soil is workable (book p. 341).
Lift in September-October, or in April before tubers regrow (book p. 342).

name: Swede
notes: Needs sun, well-drained moisture-retentive soil and early, sparse thinning or roots stay small.
Moderate nitrogen needs; same pests as cabbage, and clubroot can stop swede growing entirely.
Store cool in sacks or a root cellar over winter.
description: Often called the only truly Swedish vegetable, though it probably came from the Middle East. Grown in Scandinavia and Russia since the 1500s; its US name, rutabaga, comes from a Swedish dialect word.
howToEat: Harvest when grapefruit-sized and store cool in sacks, a root cellar or clamp over winter.

events.note: Sow direct once the soil is workable; sow in July for winter storage roots (book p. 344).
Lift when grapefruit-sized; tolerates autumn frost (book p. 344).

name: Parsley
notes: Needs deep, loose, fertile soil like carrots; fails on heavy clay.
Soak seed and mark rows with radish since seedlings are slow; feed in high summer as roots grow in autumn.
Store in damp sand somewhere cool; carrot fly is the only likely pest.
description: A root much smaller than parsnip, with leaves that look and taste like flat-leaf parsley. It came to Sweden in the 1700s but is still unknown to most people.
howToEat: A few pieces in soup give a rich taste of parsley and celery. The bigger the root, the better the flavour. A few leaves can be picked like parsley.

events.note: Sow direct when the soil is workable; soak seed and cover with fleece (book p. 360).
Lift in late autumn before the ground freezes; bigger roots taste better (book p. 360).

name: Celeriac
notes: Very demanding: rich, deep, moist soil and lots of potassium; a little wood ash helps.
Mulch, ideally with seaweed, and liquid-feed in summer. In August trim surface roots off the top of the bulb.
Cover with fleece at planting against carrot and celery fly.
description: A brown, knobbly root bred from wild sea-shore celery in the Mediterranean in the 1500s. Swedes weren't impressed when it arrived in the 1700s.
howToEat: Classic in meat soup. Store like carrots. The inner leaves can be dried and used as a herb or in tea blends.

events.note: Start indoors in February; seed needs light, so barely cover it (book p. 361).
Plant out late May-June once the soil is warm, stem base at soil level (book p. 361).
Lift in late autumn; a mulch of hay or leaves delays ground freezing (book p. 361).

name: Radish
notes: Needs loose, moist soil and a bit more feeding than radish; grass-clipping mulch keeps moisture even.
Early sowing makes it bolt, so sow in midsummer. Same pests as radish (flea beetle).
Lift before fully grown; keeps a couple of months in damp sand. Peel off the peppery skin.
description: The mother of the radish, grown in East Asia for thousands of years. The roots are bigger than radishes, with a sharper taste and coarser skin.
howToEat: The pepperiness sits in the skin, so peel before eating. The roots keep a couple of months in damp sand, and some varieties are grown for their seed pods too.

events.note: Sow direct end of June or early July to avoid bolting (book p. 365).
Lift before fully grown; roots are cold-hardy (book p. 365).

name: Radish
notes: Long roots need deep, loose soil or a raised ridge; keep moist with grass-clipping mulch.
Sow a week or two after black radish to avoid bolting; thin to 20 cm.
Lift before fully grown and store in damp sand for a couple of months.
description: A form of black radish shaped like a giant white icicle, juicier, more tender and sweeter than ordinary black radish. In China and Japan it matters as much as carrots do here.
howToEat: Peel before eating, as the peppery taste is in the skin. Best harvested before fully grown; it keeps a couple of months in damp sand.

events.note: Sow direct in July, 1-2 weeks after black radish, to avoid bolting (book p. 365).
Lift before fully grown; roots are cold-hardy (book p. 365).

name: Scorzonera
notes: Needs sun and deep, loose, humus-rich soil at least 30-40 cm deep, or roots fork.
Weed early and feed with grass clippings in high summer; keep moist to avoid mildew.
Dig alongside the brittle roots rather than pulling; broken roots lose flavour and won't store.
description: A perennial with long, slender roots, black outside and white inside, and yellow flowers. From the Mediterranean, it's nicknamed 'poor man's asparagus' for its prized flavour.
howToEat: The brittle roots are eaten peeled; store them like carrots. The leaves are also good, but only in early summer.

events.note: Sow direct once the soil has warmed (book p. 371).
Lift from October, or in April the next spring before flowering (book p. 371).

name: Salsify
notes: Needs sun and deep, loose, humus-rich soil 20-30 cm deep; stones or compaction make roots fork.
Weed early and feed with grass clippings in high summer; keep moist to avoid mildew.
Dig alongside the brittle roots rather than pulling; store like carrots.
description: A biennial with long, slender, pale yellow roots, white inside, and purple flowers. Its flavour earned it the nickname 'vegetable oyster'.
howToEat: The roots are eaten peeled and stored like carrots. The leaves are also good, but only in early summer.

events.note: Sow direct once the soil has warmed (book p. 371).
Lift from October, or in April the next spring before flowering (book p. 371).

name: Chinese artichoke
notes: Grow like Jerusalem artichoke but in more porous soil and a warmer spot; move it every year.
Lift every tuber at harvest or it turns into a weed. Low yield, about 1 kg per square metre.
description: A perennial from China with tiny tubers that look like little white porcelain sumo wrestlers. It caused a brief craze in Sweden in the late 1800s.
howToEat: Fun served in a stew or stir-fry. Luckily the tubers don't need peeling.

events.note: Start a few tubers in a pot in March or April (book p. 373).
Plant out when the soil has warmed (book p. 373).
Lift in autumn or spring (book p. 373).

name: Horseradish
notes: Give it good deep soil; plant a long side root with the thick end just below the surface.
In late June expose the root and rub off side roots except the lowest, then re-cover.
Lift all small root pieces at harvest or it spreads as a weed.
description: A hardy perennial with long, pungent roots and a fiery taste. Feral plants are common in old Swedish cottage gardens, but their roots are of poor quality.

foraging.picking: Introduced as a spice in the Middle Ages and now also found wild. Dig up the root, wash and grate it fresh; roots over a year old are often woody.
foraging.identification: Large green tongue-shaped leaves with toothed edges, thick root with a peppery smell.

events.note: Plant root cuttings once the soil is workable (book p. 373).
Lift roots in autumn or leave them until spring (book p. 373).

name: Rampion
notes: Never becomes a weed, unlike its relative creeping bellflower. Small white roots taste like a stronger radish; yield is tiny.
description: A biennial bellflower brought to Sweden by King Karl IX, who grew it on his royal estates. Its white roots are about 5 cm long and taste like radish, but a bit stronger.
howToEat: The roots are eaten boiled or raw.

events.note: Sow direct in spring, or start indoors (book p. 374).
Lift the small roots in autumn; book gives no exact time.

name: Burdock
notes: Grow and harvest like scorzonera in deep, loose soil.
Young stems and leaves are edible, but take only a few or the root stops growing.
description: A long burdock root, brown outside and white inside, loved in Japan. It tastes like globe artichoke with a subtle bitterness.
howToEat: Used the same way as scorzonera. Young stems and leaves can be eaten like chard.

events.note: Sow direct once the soil has warmed, as for scorzonera (book p. 374).
Lift in autumn, or the next spring before it flowers (book p. 374).

name: Root chervil
notes: Sow in good, loose soil; autumn sowing with fresh seed works best.
Tubers are strawberry-sized; lift when leaves die back, or overwinter and lift early spring before regrowth.
description: A biennial with small tubers like mini turnips, no bigger than strawberries, and a rich, full flavour. It was abandoned in the early 1900s and never improved by breeding.

events.note: Sow fresh seed direct in autumn (book p. 374).
Lift the small tubers when the foliage dies down in late summer (book p. 374).

name: Skirret
