notes: Tough, hardy perennial for deep, light soil; easiest started from a bought plant.
Each plant forms a cluster of pencil-thin sweet roots; divide to share or increase.
description: A tough, hardy perennial that forms a tangle of about fifty pencil-thin roots tasting of parsnip and carrot. Its high sugar content made it popular in the 1600s.

events.note: Plant a bought plant or division in spring; it can also be sown (book p. 375).
Book gives no harvest time; lift some roots in autumn like other roots.

name: Turnip
notes: Grow like turnip; flat violet roots sit on top of the soil.
A little wood ash in the soil suits it. Harvest at 6-8 cm across.
description: An antique turnip brought to Sweden by Finnish settlers, who sowed it on burnt slash-and-burn land. Its flat, round, purple roots grow on top of the soil and have a very special, powerful taste.
howToEat: Makes a memorable soup with a little cream.

events.note: Sow direct like turnip, in spring or late summer (book p. 375).
Pull when roots are 6-8 cm across (book p. 375).

name: Celery
notes: Needs sun and loose, rich, humus-rich soil that never dries out; mulch, ideally with seaweed.
Feed again in July. Blanch from August by earthing up, straw or a bottomless can, or grow a self-blanching variety.
Pests as celeriac (carrot and celery fly); harvest before it bolts.
description: An Italian creation descended from wild celery, grown for its crisp, tasty stalks. It reached Sweden in the late 1700s, and home-grown stalks are usually less crunchy than shop-bought ones.
howToEat: Eat the crisp, tender stalks, which snap easily when well grown. The leaves can always be used as a herb.

events.note: Start indoors Feb-Mar; barely cover, seed needs light. Grow on at about 16 C (book p. 376).
Plant out when nights stay at 12 C or more, or it may bolt (book p. 376).
Harvest about a month after blanching starts in August (book p. 377).

name: Artichoke
notes: Needs a warm, sunny spot and deep, loose, very rich soil; liquid-feed several times in summer.
Cut heads when the bract tips start to turn outwards; soak in water to drive out insects.
Hose off aphids in the shoot tips.
description: A perennial thistle, 100–120 cm tall, grown for its edible flower heads. Swedes grew it from the 1600s into the 1900s, and an old Swedish manor-house variety gives small but very tasty heads.
howToEat: Eat the flower heads. After cutting, soak them in water so any insects crawl out.

events.note: Start indoors Jan-early Feb; pot on and grow cooler at 12-18 C (book p. 378).
Plant out once frost risk is over, after 20 May (book p. 378).
Cut heads as bracts open; finish by late September (book p. 379).

name: Sweetcorn
notes: Needs deep, rich soil in a sunny, sheltered spot; plant in square blocks, not rows, for pollination.
Keep supersweet varieties at least 100 m from ordinary corn. Water in drought and liquid-feed twice in summer.
Cover with fleece after planting out; pick when silks wither and kernels are creamy.
description: A tall grass that Columbus brought from the Americas to Europe, where it spread worldwide within decades. In Sweden it's grown for its sweet cobs, and also for popcorn.
howToEat: Cobs are best boiled fresh. Blanch them before freezing. Popcorn varieties can be grown for popping.

imageCredit.author: The original Uploader was wstoakLL at English Wikipedia

events.note: Sow 2 seeds per 10 cm pot 3-4 weeks before planting out (book p. 379).
Plant out after frost risk once soil is at least 12 C; cover with fleece (book p. 380).
Pick when silks have withered and kernels are creamy; finish by late September (book p. 380).

name: Asparagus
notes: Needs sun and light, deep soil cleared of perennial weeds; double-dig and add plenty of compost.
Plant crowns in 30 cm trenches with a central ridge, filling in through summer; feed yearly after harvest.
Cut down in autumn. Earth up or add sand in spring for white spears.
description: A long-lived perennial that sends up finger-thick, juicy shoots each spring, then grows into a feathery hedge. It has been grown for over 5,000 years, including by the Egyptians, and comes as white (blanched) or green.
howToEat: Eat the young spring shoots. Green asparagus tastes just as good as white, and some varieties, like Primaverde, are good raw in salads.

events.note: Soak seed 1-2 days and sow in pots indoors at about 20 C (book p. 382).
Plant the seedlings into the prepared trench once frost is over (after 20 May).
Seed-grown plants need longer to establish than bought crowns before the first cutting. Then cut spears at 18–20 cm until midsummer. Most people buy crowns (book p. 382).
Plant crowns in trenches when the soil is workable (book p. 383).
Cut spears at 18-20 cm until midsummer; start 3 years after planting crowns (book p. 383).

name: Cardoon
notes: Grow like artichoke; perennial but treated as annual, 1-2 m tall with silvery leaves.
Blanch stems for a month before harvest by wrapping in corrugated card; strip coarse strings before cooking.
description: The ancestor of the artichoke: a striking plant one to two metres tall with silvery leaves, grown for its stalks. It was common in grand 1800s kitchen gardens.
howToEat: Strip the tough strings from the blanched stalks, as with rhubarb. Italians boil them and eat them with olive oil and herb butter.

events.note: Start indoors as for artichoke (book p. 386).
Plant out once frost risk is over, after 20 May (book p. 386).
Blanch from late August and harvest in September before frost risk.

name: Angelica
notes: Wants rich, loose, moist soil in a not too warm spot.
Flowers in year two then dies; collect seed and resow, and it often self-seeds.
Peel stems like rhubarb; blanching makes them more tender.
description: A tall plant that grows wild in the Swedish mountains, where the Sami once harvested its young leaves and shoots. Its stalks taste slightly sweet.
howToEat: Peel the stalks, like rhubarb, and eat them; candied stalks are a delicious treat. Young leaves and shoots can be eaten raw or boiled, the leaves make tea, and boiled flowers were eaten like cauliflower.

events.note: Sow fresh seed direct in autumn (book p. 387).
Cut young stems before flowering (book p. 387).

name: Sea kale
notes: Protected in the wild, so never dig plants; buy seed such as Lily White.
Plant in deep, loose, well-fed soil. Force in spring under an upturned bucket for 5-6 weeks.
Usually overwinters in central Sweden but not always; keep seed in reserve.
description: A perennial coastal plant that grows wild in southern Sweden, where it is protected in many places. Its blanched leaf stalks turn pale yellow and tender.
howToEat: The blanched leaf stalks are eaten as an early spring treat, in the same class as asparagus.

events.note: Sow fresh seed in pots in autumn and leave outside under fleece for the cold (book p. 387).
Plant out in deep, loose, well-fed soil (book p. 387).
Cut blanched shoots at 15 cm, from two years after sowing (book p. 387).

name: Aubergine
notes: Grow like tomato but warmer; ideal day temperature 22 C or more, so best in a pot in the greenhouse.
Liquid-feed every other week once flowering and pot on into a bucket-sized container.
Hose daily against whitefly and aphids; pick before the skin loses its gloss.
description: A heat-loving plant from India with woolly grey-green leaves and lavender-blue flowers. Fruits can be small and green, or white and egg-shaped (hence 'eggplant'), but modern varieties are mostly large and dark purple.
howToEat: Only the fruit is eaten; the leaves are poisonous.

events.note: Sow indoors in February or early March; give a sunny window and grow light (book p. 388).
Move out when nights stay at 12 C or more, in a pot in the greenhouse (book p. 388).
Pick at full size while the skin is still glossy (book p. 390).

name: Ground cherry
notes: Grow like tomato in a sunny, warm spot, in the ground or a bucket; 60-100 cm tall.
Hardier than tomato. Fruit is ripe when the husk yellows and berries drop.
description: A bushy North American plant, 60–100 cm tall, with golden berries wrapped in a papery lantern. The berries are sweet with a wild aroma.
howToEat: Best eaten fresh, and used in cakes, pies and other desserts. Eat only fully ripe berries with the papery husk removed; unripe berries are poisonous.

events.note: Sow indoors as for tomato, 8-10 weeks before planting out (book p. 394, 400).
Plant out after 20 May in a warm, sunny spot or a bucket (book p. 400).
Pick when husks turn yellow and fruit falls; finish by late September (book p. 400).

name: Tomatillo
notes: Grow like a bush tomato in the greenhouse or a sheltered spot, ideally in a large, well-fed bucket.
Prune if too bushy. Pick fruit green and unripe, mainly for salsa verde.
description: A relative of the ground cherry, taller and with fruits almost twice the size, each inside a papery husk. The flavour is a bit like tomato, but very much its own.
howToEat: Pick the fruits green and blend with coriander, onion, chilli and garlic for salsa verde. Also good in meat sauce, but not raw in salads.

events.note: Sow indoors as for tomato, 8-10 weeks before planting out (book p. 394, 400).
Plant in a large bucket in the greenhouse (book p. 400).
Pick green; fairly frost-tolerant and crops into autumn (book p. 401).

name: Arctic bramble
notes: Plant two or more varieties for pollination, in moist, loose soil rich in compost; pH matters little.
Water well during flowering and fruit set, feed lightly after year two, and renew the patch from runners every 5-8 years.
Shares pests such as the raspberry beetle with raspberry and blackberry, so keep it away from them; too much nitrogen invites grey mould.
description: A cross between wild arctic bramble and its Alaskan relative that spreads into a pretty ground cover with pink flowers. The dark red berries taste almost as heavenly as wild ones; yields are highest in the north.
howToEat: Pick when dark red and slightly soft; makes an exquisite liqueur and jam (book p. 470).

events.note: Plant in spring once the soil is workable (book p. 470).
Or plant in early autumn (book p. 470); new runners can also be moved in autumn.
Flowers early June, berries a month later (book p. 470); expect 1-3 weeks later in Stockholm. Full crop from year three.

recommendedVarieties.name: Linda
recommendedVarieties.pollination: Plant at least two of these varieties

recommendedVarieties.name: Anna
recommendedVarieties.pollination: Plant at least two of these varieties

recommendedVarieties.name: Beata
recommendedVarieties.pollination: Plant at least two of these varieties

recommendedVarieties.name: Sofia
recommendedVarieties.pollination: Plant at least two of these varieties

name: Blackberry
notes: Needs a warm spot, ideally against a south wall, in deep, light, well-drained soil; tie canes to a wire trellis with wires 30 cm apart.
Keep first-year canes on the ground (cover them in winter with spruce branches or straw) and fan-train second-year canes; cut fruited canes out in autumn, leaving 6-8 new ones.
Grey mould is the main problem: thin the canes and avoid excess nitrogen. Raspberry beetle larvae can also attack.
description: A rambling cane fruit that grows wild up to the Mälaren valley; gardens now mainly grow thornless varieties. Canes fruit in their second year and the harvest runs through autumn.

events.note: Plant in spring in a warm, sheltered spot; cut bare-root plants back to 30 cm (book p. 471).
Or plant in early autumn so it roots before the freeze; the book favours August-September (p. 466).
Harvest continues all autumn, but in cool summers not all berries ripen (book p. 471); frost risk from late September in Stockholm.

name: Blueberry
notes: Needs acid soil (pH 4-5.5): fill a 30 cm deep, 60 cm wide hole (deeper and wider in clay) with unfertilised peat mixed with composted bark, or rhododendron soil, and mulch with conifer litter.
Plant two varieties for better pollination, prune to 30 cm at planting, and after three years cut out about a fifth of the oldest and drooping branches each year.
Keep the soil constantly moist and protect flowers from frost with fleece; net against birds, hares and deer.
description: Garden blueberries taste milder and sweeter than wild ones, are two to three times larger and have white flesh that won't stain your mouth. Highbush is the commonest type, giving 2-7 kg per bush, with orange-red autumn colour.
howToEat: The berries are firm and can be eaten fresh or frozen individually (book p. 472).

events.note: Plant in spring, no deeper than in the pot, in a sunny, acid bed (book p. 474).
Or plant in autumn (book p. 474), early enough to root before the freeze.
The book gives no month; midsummer to late summer is an estimate for Stockholm.

name: Blueberry
notes: Needs acid soil (pH 4-5.5): plant in a hole filled with unfertilised peat and composted bark, or rhododendron soil, raised slightly above ground; mulch with conifer litter.
Plant at least two varieties for pollination, prune to 30 cm at planting, and after three years remove about a fifth of the oldest branches yearly.
Keep moist, cover flowers if frost threatens, and net against birds, hares and deer.
description: A cross between highbush and wild blueberry: lower (60-100 cm), slightly less productive and wilder in flavour, but more cold-hardy than highbush. Balsgård in Skåne bred the hardy variety Putte.
howToEat: The berries are firm and can be eaten fresh or frozen individually (book p. 472).

events.note: Plant in spring, no deeper than in the pot, in a sunny, acid bed (book p. 474).
Or plant in autumn (book p. 474), early enough to root before the freeze.
The book gives no month; midsummer to late summer is an estimate for Stockholm.

name: Haskap
notes: Not self-pollinating: plant two or three varieties in sun and moist soil rich in organic matter; avoids heavy clay.
Feed moderately with manure in spring; no pruning for the first 5-6 years, then thin like a currant bush.
Very healthy, but can get fungal disease in too much shade. Flowers early but tolerate about -7 to -8 °C.
description: A blue honeysuckle transformed by 60 years of Canadian and Russian breeding into a large, sweet-tart, very vitamin-rich berry. Extremely hardy, and it ripens about a week before strawberries.
howToEat: The berries are used just like blueberries and other garden berries (book p. 476).

events.note: Plant once the soil is workable; berry bushes can go in as soon as you can dig (book p. 466).
Or plant in early autumn so it roots before the freeze; the book favours August-September (p. 466).
Ripens about a week before strawberries (book p. 476); late June to early July in Stockholm.

name: Saskatoon
notes: Self-fertile but needs insects to pollinate; grows in most well-drained, porous soils in sun or light shade.
Top new plants to 25-30 cm for more branches; start pruning after 6-7 years, removing 20% of the oldest and drooping branches yearly.
Water in drought or the berries drop; birds are the only real pest.
description: A North American relative of the serviceberry, used for centuries as food and medicine from Maine to Alaska. Clouds of white blossom, orange-red autumn leaves, and berries tasting of wild blueberry with a hint of blackcurrant.
howToEat: Eat the berries when they turn from pink to dark purple; they taste like wild blueberries with a touch of blackcurrant and were long used as food by Native Americans (book p. 478).

events.note: Plant once the soil is workable; berry bushes can go in as soon as you can dig (book p. 466).
Or plant in early autumn so it roots before the freeze; the book favours August-September (p. 466).
Ripens early to mid July (book p. 478), likely mid to late July in Stockholm; pick when berries turn dark purple.

name: Sea buckthorn
notes: Female plants need a male nearby for wind pollination: one male per five females. Plant in full sun; light soil is best, lighten heavy clay.
Nitrogen-fixing and drought-tolerant, so feed sparingly but water for bigger crops. Roots spread aggressively, so plant in a corner and chop runners.
Prune to 40-50 cm at planting; protect young shoots from hares and deer with netting.
description: A tough shrub with silvery leaves and very sour orange berries tasting of passion fruit and pineapple. The berries hold three times as much vitamin C as oranges.
howToEat: Too sour to eat raw without sugar; use for parfait, sorbet, panna cotta, marmalade, cordial or a fresh-pressed health shot. Easiest harvest: cut whole branches, freeze them and shake the berries off (book p. 484).

foraging.picking: Grows wild along the coasts, especially the Baltic. Thorny and dense. Best method: clip off part of a berry-laden branch, freeze it briefly, then knock the berries off with a stick; hand-picking is slow and the berries burst easily.
foraging.habitat: Stony shores; dislikes competition from other trees and shrubs.
foraging.identification: 50-300 cm tall, bushy, with narrow silvery grey-green leaves, long sharp thorns and orange berries.
foraging.safety: Long, sharp thorns.

events.note: Spring planting is safest (book p. 484).
Potted plants can also go in in autumn (book p. 484).
The book gives no month; late summer to early autumn is an estimate for Stockholm. Cut whole branches and freeze.

recommendedVarieties.name: Svenne
recommendedVarieties.pollination: Pairs with Lotta; can be combined with the female Ljubitelskaja

recommendedVarieties.name: Lotta
recommendedVarieties.pollination: Pairs with Svenne

recommendedVarieties.name: Ljubitelskaja
recommendedVarieties.pollination: Female plant; combine with Svenne

name: Gooseberry
notes: Very sparing with nitrogen, which strongly encourages powdery mildew; feed with compost and potassium-rich wood ash instead.
From about year five, remove low-lying, damaged and the 3-4 oldest branches in late autumn or late winter.
Watch for gooseberry sawfly larvae, which can strip a bush quickly; pick them off by hand or use nematodes.
description: Gooseberry fever swept 1800s Sweden until powdery mildew wiped out the crops. Mildew-resistant varieties have brought a revival, and wild bushes from old homesteads can have unbeatable aroma.

events.note: Plant spring or autumn, 5 cm deeper than before; cut bare-root plants back to 30 cm (book p. 490).
Or plant in early autumn so roots establish before the ground freezes. Early October at the latest.
Timing not given in the book; typical summer harvest in Stockholm.

name: Lingonberry
notes: Acid-soil plant planted like blueberry; needs almost no fertiliser and too much will harm it.
Don't let it dry out, especially in June and July.
Rejuvenate after 10-15 years by cutting down to a few centimetres above the ground.
description: Cultivated lingonberries are compact evergreen plants with big red berries that taste like wild ones, making a fine edging. Each plant gives 0.5-1 litre a year from year three.

events.note: The book says plant in spring, in acid soil as for blueberries (book p. 492).
Berries ripen mid-August in the book (p. 491); allow a week or two later in Stockholm. Variety Ida repeat-flowers for a second crop.

recommendedVarieties.name: Ida
recommendedVarieties.ripening: Remontant, crops more than once per season

name: Wild strawberry
notes: Sunny spot in decent garden soil, cleared of perennial weeds and enriched with manure and compost.
Drought tolerant, but watering during fruiting raises yield; renew plants after 3-4 years from runners or by dividing alpine types.
Strawberry leaf beetle can riddle the leaves in hot, dry summers; try spraying soapy water before flowering.
description: Non-running alpine strawberries make superb edging and fruit all summer; newer runner-forming red and white types have bigger berries and are effective ground cover.

events.note: Plant in spring or early autumn (book p. 492).
Set out runners straight after harvest, or divide alpine plants, in late summer to early autumn.
Alpine types such as Rügen fruit all summer; runner types crop over a shorter period.

recommendedVarieties.name: Askungen
recommendedVarieties.pollination: First self-fertile musk strawberry

name: Tayberry
notes: Needs a warm, sunny spot, ideally trained on a south-facing wall like blackberry; cut bare-root plants back by two thirds.
Fruits on two-year canes: cut fruited canes out in autumn after harvest and lay young canes on the ground under spruce branches or straw for winter.
Gets the same pests and diseases as blackberry and raspberry.
description: A 1970s Scottish raspberry-blackberry hybrid, the best of the 'bramble-raspberries'. Deep red berries 4 cm long, on long thorny canes; keep flavour expectations modest.
howToEat: Picked when dark red and eaten fresh; the book says the berries look like jewels on a cream cake.

events.note: Plant against a sunny south wall with support in spring.
Or plant in early autumn so roots establish before the ground freezes.
Ripens a few days before raspberry, usually late July in the book (p. 494); expect late July-August in Stockholm.

name: Currant
notes: Wants full sun and moisture-retentive, humus-rich soil; feed sparingly.

Flowers on two-year-old and older wood, so start thinning after 4-5 years and prune more lightly than black currant. Prune at the base in autumn or winter: remove drooping and damaged branches and the 3-4 oldest each year.
Aphids cause reddish blisters on the leaves, mainly on red currants; spray with water or soapy water.
description: Very hardy currant grown throughout Sweden. An old Dutch red variety, around 300 years old, gives small berries but a high yield and is hardy to zone 6.

events.note: Plant spring or autumn, as for gooseberry (book p. 497).
Or plant in early autumn so roots establish before the ground freezes. Early October at the latest.
Timing not given in the book; typical mid-late summer harvest in Stockholm.

name: Currant
notes: Wants full sun and moisture-retentive, humus-rich soil; feed sparingly.
Pruned like red currant: flowers on two-year-old wood, start thinning after 4-5 years. Prune at the base in autumn or winter: remove drooping and damaged branches and the 3-4 oldest each year.
Pink currants such as Pink Champagne (a red x white cross) are grown the same way but only to zone 2.
description: White currants arose as a mutation of red currants and are slightly milder in taste, as are pink currants.

events.note: Plant spring or autumn, as for gooseberry (book p. 497).
Or plant in early autumn so roots establish before the ground freezes. Early October at the latest.
Timing not given in the book; typical mid-late summer harvest in Stockholm.

name: Elder
notes: Likes humus-rich, fertile soil; feed every spring.
Aphids love it; after a few years thin out old, woody branches.
Stands still for a few years after planting, then grows fast; good as a screen or hedge.
description: A large shrub that grows up to four metres high and wide once established. Varieties Samyl and Samidan stay at two to three metres.
howToEat: Both the flowers and the berries are used for cordial. Do not confuse it with red-berried elder (Sambucus racemosa), whose red berries are not edible (book p. 503). Always cook the berries: raw or unripe elderberries, leaves and stems can make you sick.

foraging.picking: Flowers and berries are used. The right elder has flat-topped flower clusters; check flowers, berry colour and pith before picking.
foraging.habitat: Deciduous groves and forest clearings, near farms and houses.
foraging.identification: Creamy-white, flat umbel-like flower clusters, elongated serrated leaves, black berries.

lookAlikes.name: Red-berried elder
lookAlikes.howToTell: Its flowers grow in a ball/grape-like cluster rather than flat-topped, the berries are red and the branch pith is dark; elder has flat clusters, black berries and pale pith.

lookAlikes.name: Dwarf elder
lookAlikes.howToTell: Recognised by red anthers in the flowers; must not be picked.

foraging.safety: Avoid eating raw berries, which cause stomach ache. Poisonous elders have red berries, red anthers, grape-shaped clusters or dark pith.

events.note: Plant in spring once the soil is workable (late April-May in Stockholm).
Or plant in early autumn so roots establish before the ground freezes. A sucker from a wild elder also works.
Flowers for cordial; timing not given in the book, typically around midsummer in Stockholm.
Berries for cordial; timing not given in the book.

name: Magnolia vine
notes: Usually has separate male and female plants, so buy a self-fertile (monoecious) plant if you only grow one.
Plant in porous, fertile soil in a sheltered spot, ideally against a south wall; let two shoots climb a support and feed moderately.
Propagate from side shoots; the book says sowing seed also works well.
description: Also called schisandra, the most challenging berry in the chapter: a climbing vine with lemon-scented flowers and leaves and clusters of lingonberry-red berries.
howToEat: The berries are used for cordial and a jelly said to go well with game; Siberian hunters used them against hunger and fatigue.

events.note: Plant in a sheltered, warm spot once the soil is workable; the book gives zones 1-2 (3), so it may struggle in Stockholm.
Berry clusters glow red in July-August in the book (p. 502); expect a week or two later in Stockholm.

name: Cloudberry
notes: Needs male and female plants (at least one male per nine females); only variety Nyby is self-fertile.
Recreate a bog: constantly moist, low-pH light peat mixed with reindeer lichen, ideally in a watertight basin and partial shade.
Needs almost no fertiliser; the flowers are frost-sensitive, so cover them on frosty nights.
description: A real challenge with low yields, but hardy to minus 40 degrees. New plants are easy from 10 cm rhizome pieces planted about 2 cm deep.

foraging.picking: Found on bogs and marshes, mostly in the north but as far south as Skåne. Crops vary by year and cold spoils them. Berries ripen in batches over about two months; pick one by one, as a berry picker turns them to mush.
foraging.distribution: Most common in the north; sparse throughout Sweden except Skåne and Öland.
foraging.identification: The orange, cloud-shaped berries.

events.note: Plant into a prepared bog bed once the soil thaws, about 25 plants per square metre; protect flowers from late frosts (risk until about 20 May).
Rhizome pieces can be planted in early autumn so they root before the freeze.
Harvest timing not given in the book.

recommendedVarieties.name: Nyby
recommendedVarieties.pollination: Only variety with both sexes on one plant; other cloudberries need separate male and female plants

name: Rose hip
scientificName: Rosa dumalis, R. rugosa, R. rubiginosa
notes: All roses give hips, but dog rose, Japanese rose and sweet briar give the most and best.
Feed and water, keep weed-free for the first three years and scatter wood ash around the bush.
description: Grow your own hips instead of buying imported ones, and enjoy the roses too. Hips are packed with vitamin C, carotene and magnesium.
howToEat: Used for rose hip soup, a Swedish classic.

harvest.note: rose hips; black overwintered hips are fine if not too soft

foraging.picking: Common wild rose along roadsides and hedges with large hips that are easy to pick. Wear gloves. Black hips in autumn taste as good as red ones; just avoid very soft, sticky ones.
foraging.distribution: Along the coast up to the Gulf of Bothnia.
foraging.identification: Large matt pink flowers and dark green leaves.

lookAlikes.name: Other roses
lookAlikes.howToTell: All are edible.

foraging.safety: Wear gloves: the thorns can cause nasty finger infections.

events.note: Plant in spring once the soil is workable (late April-May in Stockholm).
Or plant in early autumn so roots establish before the ground freezes.
Pick when bright red, ideally before the first frost nights (book p. 505); frost risk in Stockholm from about 25 September.

name: Black chokeberry
notes: Grown like black currant.
Robust and healthy; variety Hugin is hardy to zone 4.
description: The black berries taste of almost nothing but are rich in acid and dark pigment. Also an attractive ornamental with leaves that turn bright red in autumn.
howToEat: Useful for jelly and cordial thanks to their acidity and colour.

events.note: Plant as for black currant in spring.
Or plant in early autumn so roots establish before the ground freezes. Early October at the latest.
Harvest timing not given in the book.

name: Anise
notes: Needs light, porous but not poor soil; thin to 20 cm and keep weeds down.
Grows best around 20 °C and needs a warm summer for the seeds to ripen, so starting indoors is the safer bet in Stockholm.
description: A graceful plant with feathery leaves and pink flowers, grown only for its liquorice-flavoured seeds. A medicinal plant since antiquity, mostly prescribed for coughs.
howToEat: Only the seeds are used: in cough sweets, schnapps and bread, and a pinch is good in fish soup or nettle soup.

events.note: Sow direct once the soil is workable and warm; mid-May in Stockholm, later than the book's 'when the soil is ready' (book p. 419).
Optional head start: starting indoors gives a better chance of ripe seed (book p. 419).
Harden off and plant out after about 20 May.
Hang plants to dry indoors over newspaper to catch the falling seeds (book p. 419).

name: Anise hyssop
notes: Sunny spot with porous, fertile soil; needs more nutrients and moisture than most herbs.
Perennial but does not always survive winter; it usually self-seeds.
Grows well in a pot on a balcony if the pot is at least 30 cm across.
description: A mildly scented perennial tasting of anise with a hint of mint, flowering June to August. Long grown by Native Americans, its flowers are a superb nectar source for butterflies and bees.
howToEat: Flowers and leaves are used, fresh or dried, in salads and tea or with chicken and pork. Pick leaves before flowering and flowers just as they open.

events.note: Sow indoors; seeds germinate readily and seedlings are sturdy (book p. 420).
Harden off and plant out after frost risk, from about 20 May (book p. 420).
May flower the first year or the next; leaves before flowering, flowers as they open (book p. 420).

name: Basil
notes: Needs lots of warmth, light and sun; outside southern Sweden the book recommends growing it in pots (at least 20 cm wide) that go out in summer.
Use porous, rich soil, water sparingly and liquid-feed all season; shower off aphids and let the soil dry slightly to deter fungus gnats.
To delay flowering, cut the plant back to two or three leaf pairs once it has six to eight; pinching buds does not work.
description: A culinary icon, once sacred to the Romans and the base of Genoese pesto. Its flavour comes from linalool (floral), methyl chavicol (anise) and eugenol (clove) in varying balance between varieties.
howToEat: The leaves are used fresh or dried in tomato, rice and pasta dishes and snipped into salads; basil with garlic always works. Blitz leaves with olive oil and freeze as a pesto base.

events.note: Sow from late Feb/March with a south window or grow light, otherwise April; keep warm until germination (book p. 423).
Pot on several seedlings per pot at the first true leaves, then into bigger pots as roots fill them (book p. 423).
Harden off and move out only when nights stay around 15 °C, usually June in Stockholm; pots are the safer option (book p. 423).
Cut sprigs as needed; bring pots back in before autumn frost (book p. 423-425).

name: Spignel
notes: Sunny spot with light, porous soil; do not let it suffer drought, especially in late summer when it withers.
Very hardy: the author reports it overwintering in Norrbotten.
Clip it into a neat ball after flowering.
description: A forgotten herb that arrived in Sweden in the 1600s, with airy dill-like leaves and sweet white umbels. Related to parsley and sometimes grown in rock gardens for its foliage.
howToEat: The leaves are used like parsley, snipped over food, and also as a schnapps and fish seasoning.

events.note: Start indoors in March; alternatively sow in autumn in a shallow, well-drained box left outside under fleece (book p. 425-426).
Plant out hardened seedlings in May.
Pick leaves as needed.
Buy a plant or divide an existing one (book p. 426).
Pick leaves as needed.

name: Perilla
notes: Loose soil and a sunny spot; frost kills it.
Seeds are covered thinly and germinate slowly and unevenly; direct sowing needs fleece at first.
Water in drought and liquid-feed a couple of times in summer, or mulch with grass clippings.
description: Japan's and Korea's parsley, in green (shiso) and red forms. Green is the most aromatic, tasting of cumin, coriander, mint and lemon at once; red has crinkled purple leaves and a milder taste.
howToEat: The leaves are used fresh, in sushi and with fish; Koreans fill the large leaves with food. Red leaves are made into tea.

events.note: Raise plants indoors (book p. 427).
Frost-tender: plant out only after 20 May.
Pinch or cut young shoots as needed; finish before late-September frost (book p. 427).

name: Fenugreek
notes: Needs sun, warmth and loose soil; unlike coriander it does not tolerate frost.
Cover with fleece after sowing and water in drought, or it bolts.
description: Essential in Persian cooking and loved in India. Its bittersweet taste recalls a freshly mown meadow, and the ground seeds go into many curry blends.
howToEat: Leaves and seeds are used; the leaves dry well and go into curries and chapati. Seeds rarely ripen in Sweden, but if they do, grind them for curry mix.

events.note: Sow direct only when the soil is about 12 °C, late May at the earliest in Stockholm; resow after harvest like coriander (book p. 427).
Harvest at about 30 cm before any sign of flowering; if it bolts, harvest everything at once (book p. 427).

name: Lemongrass
notes: Tender perennial: grow in a pot of rich soil outside in a sunny, sheltered spot in summer and bring it in before frost.
Overwinter like a pelargonium, bright and cool with very little water; trim dead leaves, repot and divide in spring.
Stalks only swell in the second year, so overwintering is needed for a real crop.
description: A perennial grass inseparable from Thai food, with lemon flavour in both stalks and leaves. Impossible outdoors in Sweden but grows into a nearly metre-high clump in a pot.
howToEat: Stems and leaves are used: the white stalks are chopped finely, and leaves (fresh or dried) are cooked like bay leaves and removed. Never chew fresh blades, as grass can stick in your throat.

events.note: Sow indoors; the book says it is hardly worth it unless you cannot get plants (book p. 428).
Move the pot outside after 20 May to a sunny, sheltered spot.
Use leaves the first year; stalks thicken in year two.
Bring in by late September; dies at -4 °C. Keep bright and cool with very little water over winter (book p. 428).
Root shop-bought stalks with some base left in a glass of water, then pot up; or buy a plant (book p. 428).
Pot outside after 20 May.
Cut stalks and leaves as needed.
Overwinter bright, cool and almost dry (book p. 428).

name: Lemon balm
notes: Best in loose, fertile soil that never dries out; may need winter cover in colder areas and can turn weedy in the south.
After a midsummer harvest cut it back by half; feed or mulch with grass clippings if regrowth is slow.
Renew by division or sowing after three or four years; watch for aphids and hose them off.
description: A mildly lemony, sweetly scented herb from the Mediterranean, adored by bees and easy for beginners. Its leaves contain calming compounds, hence the old Swedish name meaning 'heart's delight'.
howToEat: The leaves are used, best fresh, in desserts, summer drinks, chicken, fish and marinades. For drying, harvest just before flowering.

events.note: Sow indoors and cover thinly or the seeds won't germinate (book p. 429).
Plant out after frost risk, from mid/late May.
Pick leaves all summer; they coarsen in midsummer, so cut back (book p. 429).
Propagate by cuttings or by dividing old plants (book p. 429).
Pick leaves as needed.

name: Lemon verbena
notes: Tender woody shrub from South America: grow in a pot and overwinter indoors in a cool, bright window, like lemongrass.
Prune it back to keep it bushy and attractive.
Propagate by cuttings in spring or autumn.
description: No plant has such an exclusive lemon flavour; the whole plant smells and tastes strongly. Dry branches tossed on the fire scent the whole room.
howToEat: The leaves are used fresh or dried in drinks, dressings, jellies, fruit salads and desserts, or to line a sponge-cake tin. Unless finely chopped, remove them before serving.

events.note: Move the potted plant outside after 20 May.
Leaves taste best just after the plant starts flowering (book p. 430).
Bring in by late September and overwinter cool and bright (book p. 430).

name: Chervil
notes: Porous, reasonably fertile soil; never let it dry out.
Prefers partial shade, as it bolts quickly in strong sun; sowing between vegetable rows suits it and saves space.
description: Looks like flat-leaf parsley with white umbels and tastes of parsley and anise. Called Swedish chervil in the 1800s, but the Danes kept making chervil soup, so the name moved.
howToEat: The leaves are used fresh like parsley; add them at the end of cooking, as they lose flavour if boiled.

events.note: Sow direct in rounds all summer from late April, ideally in part shade (book p. 431).
Cut or pinch young shoots as needed (book p. 431).

name: Sweet cicely
notes: One of the few herbs that happily grows in shade; very vigorous and long-lived.
Cut off the seed heads to stop it becoming a weed.
description: A metre-tall perennial with fern-like leaves and an anise flavour; colonies survive for generations around old ruins and homesteads.
howToEat: The leaves are used mainly in spring and early summer; if too liquorice-like, use them as a garnish or add a sprig to spinach or vegetable soups.

foraging.picking: Pick the whole plant at the base or take leaves, flowers or seed pods separately. Keep the delicate leaves in an inflated plastic bag. Confirm by the anise smell.
foraging.habitat: Cultivated land: old settlements, roadsides and parks.
foraging.identification: 60-120 cm with upright stem, large, triangular, repeatedly divided light green leaves, often white-flecked and hairy, smelling strongly of anise/liquorice when rubbed.

lookAlikes.name: Cowbane
lookAlikes.howToTell: Same family and very poisonous; only pick if completely sure, and do not touch a plant lacking the anise and liquorice smell.

lookAlikes.name: Hemlock
lookAlikes.howToTell: Same family and very poisonous; sweet cicely is identified by its anise and liquorice smell.

lookAlikes.name: Fool's parsley
lookAlikes.howToTell: Same family and very poisonous; sweet cicely is identified by its anise and liquorice smell.

foraging.safety: Not for beginners. Only pick if completely sure; never touch a plant lacking the anise/liquorice smell.

events.note: Sow fresh seed in autumn in a shallow box covered with fleece and left outside all winter; spring sowings need 3-4 weeks of cold first (book p. 432).
Plant out as soon as seedlings have a couple of leaf pairs (book p. 432).
Leaves are best in spring and early summer; some harvest possible the first summer.

name: Tarragon
notes: Needs well-drained, humus-rich soil; divide every fourth year or the flavour declines.
Overwinters in southern and central Sweden and even in parts of Norrbotten; cut down fully in late spring and hose off aphids.
description: The tarragon of béarnaise sauce. French tarragon is sterile, so any seed sold as tarragon is not the French kind; the hardier Russian type is a little taller and bitter-lemony.
howToEat: The leaves are used fresh, dried or frozen. Russian tarragon mixed with lovage makes a good soup seasoning.

events.note: Buy a plant, as French tarragon cannot be sown; also propagates from tip cuttings (book p. 432).
Pick leaves as needed.

name: Hyssop
notes: Needs only a few hours of sun, light well-drained soil and very little feeding; can form a low hedge (15-20 cm apart, otherwise double).
Top plants when planting out so they branch, and cut back by nearly half each spring, never into old wood.
After four or five years it gets woody: dig up and divide in spring.
description: The 'lavender of the north': a bushy perennial with blue flower spikes, much hardier and easier than lavender and said to have survived -43 °C. Women once sniffed a sprig in church to stay awake.
howToEat: Flowers and leaves are used: the strong, slightly bitter leaves fresh or dried with fatty fish, meat and game; flowers over potato salad or in tea.

events.note: Start indoors (book p. 434).
Plant out once the soil has warmed, late May in Stockholm; no harvest the first year (book p. 418, 434).
From year two: leaves as flowers are about to open, flowers once open (book p. 434).
Buy plants or divide old ones in spring (book p. 434).
Leaves as flowers are about to open, flowers once open.

name: Coriander
notes: Loose, moisture-retentive soil kept moist; fleece speeds up the first sowing.
Sow in rounds every two to three weeks rather than treating it like parsley; late-summer sowings give record harvests.
Thin to 5 cm for leaves or 20 cm for seed.
description: The world's most widely used herb, grown by the Egyptians 3,000 years ago. People either love or hate the taste, and it thrives in Swedish autumns.
howToEat: Leaves, seeds and root are used: leaves like parsley, especially in stir-fries with ginger and garlic; seeds in tomato dishes, curries, bread and pickles; the crushed root in stews and soups.

events.note: First sowing when the soil is warm, then every 2-3 weeks; don't miss the late-summer sowing (book p. 435).
Pinch leaves from 10 cm; harvest whole plants when top leaves turn dill-like; let bolted plants set seed (book p. 435).

name: Fennel
notes: Needs a sunny spot and well-drained, fertile soil kept moist, loose and weed-free.
A perennial that only overwinters in southern Sweden in mild winters, so treat it as an annual in Stockholm.
description: Same species as Florence fennel but without the swollen bulb, grown mainly for its seeds, a classic bread spice. Some American sects chewed the seeds to stave off hunger during long sermons.
howToEat: Seeds and leaves are used: cut the stems when the seed heads turn yellow and use the seeds in bread. Pick the feathery leaves as needed for fish dishes; bronze fennel is superb with fish and shellfish.

events.note: Sow indoors in April (book p. 436).
Plant out once the soil is warm, from late May in Stockholm (book p. 436).
Pick leaves as needed; cut seed stems when the seed heads yellow (book p. 436).

name: Sage
notes: Plant in sun in light, well-drained soil; cut back to just under half each spring for fresh growth.
Hardy to about -15 °C; in light soil, a warm spot and under spruce branches it can take more, but not the far north.
Renew after five or six years from cuttings; coloured-leaf varieties are less hardy and can't be grown from seed.
description: A silvery, downy Mediterranean sub-shrub grown in Swedish gardens since the Middle Ages, covered in blue flowers and insects in July. Eating sage was said to make you wise, and research partly agrees.
howToEat: Pick the leaves as needed; they can be dried but the flavour suffers. Classic with fatty food and meat, also good in tomato dishes; lighten it with lemon balm, mint or parsley, or brew a leaf in herbal tea.

events.note: Sow indoors in March or April and keep lightly moist; flowers only from the second year (book p. 437).
Plant out after the frost risk, from about 20 May in Stockholm (book p. 437).
Pick leaves as needed (book p. 438).
Buy plants or root cuttings; the only option for coloured-leaf varieties (book p. 437-438).
Pick leaves as needed (book p. 438).

name: Caraway
notes: Biennial: a leaf rosette the first year, pinkish-white flowers and seed in early summer of the second.
Wants sun and fertile, humus-rich, light soil; thin, water in drought and keep weeds down.
description: A biennial once exported in barrels from Skåne and still found wild on dry meadows in Sweden. Wild plants are easy to confuse with the very poisonous cowbane, which is taller and has red-flecked stems.
howToEat: Mostly seeds, plus young leaves: young fresh leaves go in salads, and the seeds flavour bread, aquavit, goulash and bean or vegetable dishes. If you forage it wild, beware of mixing it up with the very poisonous cowbane.

events.note: Sow direct once the soil is workable (book p. 439).
In year two, cut the seed heads when the capsules turn grey-brown but before they open, then dry (book p. 439).

name: Lavender
notes: Needs sun and light, very porous, well-drained soil; also thrives in a pot.
Prune by about half every spring, since it quickly turns woody.
Space 20 cm for a hedge, 40 cm otherwise; not hardy in northern Sweden.
description: A woody Mediterranean sub-shrub whose whole plant contains lavender oil, mostly in the flowers. It makes a fragrant low hedge loved by butterflies and bumblebees.
howToEat: Flowers and leaves are used, and the flowers smell best in bud. Dried flowers flavour sweet bakes, marmalade, ice cream and tea; fresh flowers garnish desserts.

events.note: Buying plants is easiest; cuttings also work (book p. 440).
Leaves and flowers all summer; flowers finest in bud, dry in bunches (book p. 440).
Sow in autumn in a seed tray covered with fleece and left outside all winter; expect only a few seedlings in spring, and hybrids won't come true (book p. 440).
Plant out the spring seedlings (book p. 440).
Light harvest once plants are established (book p. 440).

name: Lovage
notes: Plant in well-drained, moist, fertile soil in sun or part shade; yellowing usually means too little water.
Cut the whole plant down after flowering and it soon becomes neat and compact again; divide to get more.
Attracts parasitic wasps whose larvae eat aphids and other pests.
description: A robust, head-high perennial that grows far north and tastes exactly like stock, because stock is flavoured with it.
howToEat: The leaves are used, fresh or dried, in soups, marinades and stews, and they freeze well. Pick in spring and early summer before the flowers come.

events.note: Plant a bought plant or a division (book p. 442).
Pick leaves in spring and early summer before flowering (book p. 442).
Seed loses viability fast, so sow fresh seed outdoors in autumn; old seed still gives a plant or two (book p. 442).
Pick leaves from the following spring (book p. 442).

name: Wormwood
notes: Loves full sun and light, well-drained, lean soil; too much feed turns the leaves green.
Cut down to 15 cm each spring; renew by division or cuttings after four or five years.
description: A silvery, strongly scented, bitter perennial growing wild in southern Sweden, once used against moths and for stomach complaints. The drier the site, the more silvery the leaves.
howToEat: Leaves and flowers flavour vermouth and aquavit: put a top shoot in a bottle of aquavit for three or four days. Warning: wormwood contains thujone, which is poisonous in high doses, so wormwood drinks should not be taken daily.

events.note: Starting indoors in April is safest; direct sowing in May also works (book p. 443).
Plant out when the soil is warm, from late May in Stockholm (book p. 443).
Leaves all summer; flowers as they begin to open; dry in bunches (book p. 443).
Buy plants, or use divisions or cuttings (book p. 443).
Leaves all summer, flowers as they open (book p. 443).

name: Marjoram
notes: A perennial that isn't hardy here, so grow it as an annual; likes sun and humus-rich, light soil.
Harvest regularly before flowering to keep it bushy; does well in pots.
description: An oregano relative from India, grown as an annual in Sweden since the late 1500s at Nyköpingshus castle. Its flowers are tiny, but the buds look like little green cones.
howToEat: The leaves are used: pea soup demands marjoram, and it also suits tomato dishes, vegetable stews, pasta and egg dishes. Dry it in bunches.

events.note: Sow indoors in March or April; seeds germinate in light, so don't cover them, and keep moist (book p. 444).
Plant out once the soil is warm, from late May in Stockholm; direct sowing gives too short a season (book p. 444).
Harvest little and often before it flowers (book p. 444).

name: Mint
notes: Easy in sun or part shade in any well-drained soil that isn't starved; water in drought for big yields.
Invasive: plant in a bottomless bucket or at the wild edge of the garden.
Variegated mints are less pushy but more tender and don't always overwinter.
description: Around thirty Mentha species that cross freely, even in your garden, so new hybrids keep appearing. Menthol in the leaves gives the flavour; spearmint, not peppermint, is the great culinary mint worldwide.
howToEat: The leaves are used. Spearmint goes in mint sauce, meat and vegetable dishes, Moroccan mint is the tastiest culinary mint, mojito mint is for drinks, and peppermint is for tea and desserts.

events.note: Buy a plant or take a cutting or a 5 cm root piece covered with a couple of centimetres of soil; most mints are hybrids, so seed is pointless (book p. 445).
Pick leaves whenever you like (book p. 445).

name: Oregano
notes: Wants a sunny, warm spot in light, well-drained soil that needn't be rich.
Cut back to 5-7 cm each spring; divide and replant old plants to rejuvenate them.
Greek oregano has the strongest flavour but is less hardy and doesn't always survive winter.
description: The pizza herb grows wild in Sweden on rocky outcrops and woodland edges, under another Swedish name. It only became a kitchen herb here when pizza culture arrived.
howToEat: The leaves are used and keep their flavour when dried. Use in pizza and all kinds of onion, tomato and minced-meat dishes, and with pork and lamb.

events.note: Sow indoors in March or April; keep lightly moist, never wet; germination is patchy (book p. 449).
Plant out after the frost risk, from about 20 May in Stockholm (book p. 449).
Pick as needed (book p. 449).
Propagate by root suckers, cuttings or division (book p. 449).
Pick as needed (book p. 449).

name: Rosemary
notes: Not hardy in Stockholm: grow in a pot of sandy soil in full sun and water in drought.
Overwinter indoors somewhere bright and cool, ideally 10-12 °C, and mist against dry indoor air; losses happen.
The creeping variety Prostrate has survived several winters on the author's Stockholm balcony.
description: Its name means 'dew of the sea'; on Mediterranean shores it becomes a woody, metre-high shrub. Greek students wore rosemary wreaths to sharpen their memory before exams.
howToEat: The leaves are used fresh or dried; fresh ones taste stronger. Pair with garlic for lamb, game, pork, chicken and fish, or use in apple cake and marmalades.

events.note: Put the potted plant outside in sun once frost is over, from about 20 May (book p. 451).
Pick leaves as needed or dry them for winter (book p. 451).
Bring the pot in before frost to a bright, cool place, ideally 10-12 °C (book p. 451).

name: Summer savory
notes: Needs full sun and loose soil without much feed; water sparingly but avoid long, extreme drought.
Gets leggy from too much nitrogen or too little light; regular picking makes it bushier. Grows well in pots.
description: A bushy annual from southern Europe with a slightly peppery taste reminiscent of oregano and thyme. The Romans steeped sprigs in vinegar and probably spread it to northern Europe.
howToEat: The leaves are used fresh or dried, traditionally with beans, cabbage and sausage. To harvest the whole plant, pull it just before it flowers.

events.note: Sow direct once the soil is warm, mid to late May in Stockholm; cover only 1-2 mm as it germinates in light (book p. 453).
Pick leaves regularly; take whole plants just before flowering (book p. 453).

name: Huacatay
notes: Excellent in the Swedish climate: one plant gives huge leaf yields, but feed it in high summer for the best leaves.
It never flowers here; sold as Mexican marigold to deter pests and soil nematodes, and it outcompetes weeds.
description: A Peruvian and Mexican herb used like coriander, with a mixed flavour of apple, mint, tarragon, lemon and basil. Many coriander haters love it despite its unflattering Swedish name.
howToEat: The leaves are used, mainly in sauces: classic huacatay sauce blends oil, leaves, lime or lemon, chilli and salt. Stuffing fish with lots of leaves is best of all; freeze surplus fresh or blended with oil.

events.note: Start indoors in April (book p. 454).
Plant out after the frost risk, from about 20 May in Stockholm (book p. 454).
Harvest in rounds all season and freeze the surplus (book p. 454).

name: Thyme
notes: Needs blazing sun and well-drained, preferably sandy soil; only compost, as too much feed makes plants too weak to overwinter.
Hates wet; cover with spruce branches or fleece against late-winter swings between sun and frost.
Divide or resow every three or four years; cuttings also work.
description: Garden thyme is the tallest, bushiest and most productive of about 350 species, a woody evergreen with pale lilac flowers from June to August. It contains thymol, once a big-selling cough remedy.
howToEat: The leaves are used fresh or dried. Harvest just as the flowers begin to open and dry the sprigs hanging somewhere dry and shady.

events.note: Sow indoors in March or April and cover very thinly; germinates in about three weeks (book p. 457).
Plant out once the soil is warm, from late May in Stockholm (book p. 457).
Harvest as the flowers begin to open (book p. 457).
Buy plants or use cuttings or divisions; the only way for species other than garden thyme (book p. 457).
Harvest as the flowers begin to open (book p. 457).

name: Rue
notes: Sun or light shade in light, well-drained soil; drought-tolerant and needs only a little compost.
Cut back in spring for fresh leaves; divide only after about ten years.
Handling it in sunshine or wet weather can cause burn-like skin irritation.
description: A Mediterranean herb with blue-green, clover-like leaves and airy yellow flowers. Medieval monks were prescribed it to dampen their libido.
howToEat: Use the fresh leaves sparingly for their biting taste, in dressings, marinades, fish, cheese and egg dishes, or snipped over potato salad. Warning: touching the leaves in sun or when wet can cause burn-like skin irritation, so handle only when dry and out of the sun.

events.note: Sow indoors in March or April; flowers the year after sowing (book p. 458, 460).
Plant out once the soil is warm, from late May in Stockholm (book p. 458).
Pick leaves as needed and use fresh (book p. 460).
Buy a plant in spring or take cuttings (book p. 458, 460).
Pick leaves as needed and use fresh (book p. 460).

name: Southernwood
notes: Hardy to at least zone 5; plant in sun or light shade in porous, well-drained soil with no feeding.
Cut back every spring but not into the old wood; divide when woody and scruffy. Can be clipped into a hedge.
description: A woody, bushy scent plant with grey-green, dill-like leaves smelling sweeter and more lemony than its relatives wormwood and tarragon. It was a staple of church posies sniffed during sermons.
howToEat: Not much of a kitchen herb: the leaves can flavour aquavit, or baked goods as the French do.

events.note: Seed is hard; root a 10 cm top-shoot cutting, which roots within days (book p. 460).
Pick leaves as needed.

name: Pineappleweed
description: A handy chamomile cousin with a pineapple flavour, worth watching for when foraging in town.
howToEat: Use the flower buds fresh with a bit of stem, or the whole plant, as a dessert herb: make syrup, or drizzle the buds in sugar syrup over strawberries.

foraging.picking: Looks like small rayless chamomile buds on a shorter plant. Tough: grows by kerbs, gravel roads and overgrown gravel yards, often in large stands. Snip at ground level and take the whole stem.
foraging.identification: Round greenish-yellow flower heads without the white ray florets of ordinary chamomile; aromatic scent.

lookAlikes.name: Scentless mayweed and relatives (Tripleurospermum)
lookAlikes.howToTell: Pineappleweed has no white ray florets, only a round yellowish flower head, and smells aromatic.

name: Greater plantain
description: Unless you need it to stop bleeding, you can sprinkle its toasted seeds on your muesli.
howToEat: Toast the seeds in a dry pan and use like linseed in muesli, porridge or bread. Eat young leaves raw in salads; blanch larger ones like spinach or use them as wraps, removing the tough midrib.

harvest.note: ripe brown seeds in late summer/autumn

foraging.picking: Grows almost everywhere, often in large stands. In autumn strip the ripe brown seeds off the stalk with your fingers. Young and older leaves both work, but young ones are much easier to chew raw.
foraging.habitat: Cultivated ground, lawns, yards, gravel roads and roadsides.
foraging.identification: Broad leaves in a basal rosette; flowers in a long, narrow spike with violet to yellow-brown anthers.

lookAlikes.name: Hoary plantain and ribwort plantain
lookAlikes.howToTell: Same genus but with coarser, hairier leaves; they can be used the same way as greater plantain.

name: Chamomile
description: One of summer's iconic flowers, and also a good flavouring with its own character.
howToEat: Use the flowers for tea, as a flavouring (e.g. in cordial) and as decoration; they taste and smell strongest when fully open.

foraging.picking: Easy to recognise and often grows in large stands. Look on earth banks and soil heaps left after forest roads are built, where the flowers are easy to spot with little competition.
foraging.identification: 20-50 cm tall with a strong aromatic scent, finely divided leaves and a conical flower head that is hollow inside.

lookAlikes.name: Oxeye daisy
lookAlikes.howToTell: Has broader ray petals.

lookAlikes.name: Scentless mayweed
lookAlikes.howToTell: Its flower centre is flat rather than pointed, and it is not hollow when the flower head is cut through.

name: Chanterelle
description: The forest's obvious gold, loved by everyone and often well hidden in the moss.
howToEat: Eat the whole mushroom fresh or pickled; freeze it blanched in its blanching water, or dry it slowly at about 40 °C to flavour mushroom soups.

foraging.picking: Easy to find and early; the pale chanterelle comes first. Likes mixed forest; often hides in moss, so feel around for more nearby. Also pops up along ditches and trodden forest paths.
foraging.identification: Entirely yellow with forked ridges running down the stem; yellowish-white flesh with a fruity smell.

lookAlikes.name: False chanterelle
lookAlikes.howToTell: Has true gills under the cap; no food value.

lookAlikes.name: Pale chanterelle
lookAlikes.howToTell: Pale in colour; a good edible mushroom.

lookAlikes.name: Meadow waxcap and woodwax (lundvaxing)
lookAlikes.howToTell: Have widely spaced gills under the cap; also edible.

foraging.safety: The book says there are no poisonous look-alikes.

name: Heather
description: A dwarf shrub, Västergötland's provincial flower, covered in lovely small purple flowers.
howToEat: Strip off the flowers and small needle-like leaves for tea or to flavour olive oil (subtle); sprigs can be used for table settings or to serve a starter on.

foraging.picking: Grows on heaths; recognised by small pale purple flowers along the whole plant. Pick during the roughly six weeks it flowers. The stem is woody, so use secateurs or a good knife. Can live up to 40 years.
foraging.habitat: Poor soil, heaths, open forest, pine bogs and rock outcrops.
foraging.identification: 20-80 cm tall with needle-like leaves and pale purple flowers.

lookAlikes.name: Cross-leaved heath
lookAlikes.howToTell: Similar leaves but urn-shaped flowers gathered in clusters.

name: Almond brittlegill
description: A personal favourite among the brittlegills, nutty and with a fine texture.
howToEat: Eat the whole mushroom cooked, with a nutty note; blanch and freeze in the cooking water, dry thinly sliced, or bake whole and serve with fish, salt, cumin and oil.

foraging.picking: Resembles other brittlegills, most of which are edible. If you are sure it is a brittlegill, taste a little: mild ones can be picked, acrid ones are no good. Brittlegill gills are brittle and break when you run a finger over them. Rarer than e.g. the herring brittlegill.
foraging.identification: Slightly sticky when damp; white stem sometimes spotted yellow or brown; brittle, widely spaced white gills like shaved almonds when detached; white flesh tasting of almond. Cap varies from brownish-yellow to chocolate brown, sometimes dark red or violet.

lookAlikes.name: Burning brittlegill (pepparkremla)
lookAlikes.howToTell: Inedible (not poisonous but unpleasant); usually has red tinges on the stem and tastes acrid.

foraging.safety: Only taste-test once you are sure the mushroom is a brittlegill; reject any that taste acrid.

name: Rosebay willowherb
description: Known by many names, including fireweed: a plant that grows in big stands and can be eaten from root to flower.
howToEat: Young shoots raw or lightly scalded like asparagus (bitter); flowers before they turn fluffy; split stems give a sweet, starchy pith for thickening sauces; leaves make tea.

foraging.picking: Grows in large stands along roadsides, ditches, clearings and meadows, and is tall, so a big harvest is easy. Once the flowers start turning to fluff the stem becomes woody and bland.
foraging.identification: 70-160 cm tall with pinkish-red flowers; leaves dark green above and paler beneath.

lookAlikes.name: Other willowherbs
lookAlikes.howToTell: Have opposite leaves, usually on the lower part of the stem.

name: Bog bilberry
description: If you think you are picking blueberries but your fingers don't turn blue, it's probably bog bilberry, the blueberry's vitamin C-packed double.
howToEat: Use the berries like blueberries: fresh, dried, or in jam and jelly. Young leaves can be eaten raw or made into tea, but in moderation.

foraging.picking: Easily confused with blueberries and grows in similar places, but seems drawn to water, often alongside bog myrtle. Berries are larger and paler, the shrub bigger, and a crushed berry doesn't stain your fingers blue.
foraging.identification: 15-70 cm tall with pale blue berries; like blueberries but much larger and they don't stain.

lookAlikes.name: Bog myrtle
lookAlikes.howToTell: Can be confused before it flowers or the berries appear; bog myrtle leaves smell very aromatic.

foraging.safety: The leaves have a laxative effect, so don't eat too many.

name: Tansy
description: A mildly poisonous flavour bomb that works especially well as a seasoning for meat.
howToEat: Use small amounts of the dried flowers/buds and leaves in a meat rub, or fry a few buds with meat; too much becomes bitter and perfumed.

harvest.note: buds and flowers; flowers from July

foraging.picking: Easy to pick on walks along fields; recognised by its smell and flower clusters. Appears in June and flowers from July. Use only small amounts.
foraging.identification: 50-150 cm tall with a strong smell, flat yellow flower heads and feathery, needle-like leaves.

lookAlikes.name: Costmary
lookAlikes.howToTell: Tansy has small needle-like leaf lobes.

foraging.safety: Mildly poisonous: contains thujone, so use only small amounts and avoid during pregnancy.

name: Red clover
description: Clover isn't just for cows; Sweden's most cultivated legume also looks great on a salad.
howToEat: Pull the small petals off the flowers and scatter over salads or rice; the flowers also make tea or flower salt and keep their colour when dried, with a light honey taste.

foraging.picking: Very common and found almost everywhere: roadsides, parks, lawns, meadows and sometimes forest. Grows up to about half a metre and flowers June to August.
foraging.identification: Straight stem without runners; three-part leaves often with pale markings.

lookAlikes.name: Zigzag clover
lookAlikes.howToTell: Has runners and a crooked stem.

name: Yarrow
description: The herbal-medicine star that has now found its way into foragers' kitchens too.
howToEat: A delicate, stringy herb best used fresh: flowers and leaves in salads or as tea. It was once used in brewing like hops.

foraging.picking: A classic healing herb with white flowers tinged purple, growing along roadsides, ditches and meadows through summer and well into autumn. Tough, so cut with a knife.
foraging.identification: 30-70 cm tall with small white flower heads, usually with five ray florets, sometimes reddish to pale pink.

lookAlikes.name: Sneezewort
lookAlikes.howToTell: Grows in damper places and has larger flowers.

name: Small-leaved lime
description: It is impressive to harvest from a tree that can live a thousand years; the creamy white flowers last well into summer.
howToEat: The sweet, slightly bitter-almond flowers make tea (said to soothe a sore throat), cordial, or can be used fresh in salads and pickled for desserts.

foraging.picking: A common tree recognised by its heart-shaped leaves and late flowers; it is the last tree to flower. Pinch the flower clusters off the twig with thumb and forefinger.
foraging.identification: Heart-shaped leaves with bluish-green undersides bearing almost rust-coloured tufts; creamy white flowers.

name: Porcini
description: Also known as the king bolete (karljohan), in many ways the perfect edible mushroom.
howToEat: Eat the whole mushroom raw in thin slices with a dip, fried, pickled, or in sauces, soups and stews; dry and grind for stock, or blend with oil into an egg-free mayonnaise.

foraging.picking: 'Karljohan' covers three similar boletes of equal food value. Recognise it by the white net on the stem, darker below and almost white near the cap. Often grows by conifers in mossy forest, frequently near fly agarics. Leave specimens attacked by the bolete mould parasite (swollen stem, tiny cap, white then yellow coating).
foraging.habitat: Mixed forest, often near pine trunks.
foraging.identification: Chubby, with a coarse net on the stem turning white towards the top; white pores that yellow with age; domed brown cap, wrinkled towards the edge.

lookAlikes.name: Bitter bolete
lookAlikes.howToTell: Extremely bitter but not poisonous; tasting a little immediately tells you it is wrong.

lookAlikes.name: Devil's bolete
lookAlikes.howToTell: Dangerous; it has red colours that signal it is not edible.

lookAlikes.name: Young fly agaric
lookAlikes.howToTell: A young fly agaric can resemble an undeveloped bolete; the problem disappears once they grow a bit larger, so take extra care with small specimens.

foraging.safety: Devil's bolete is dangerous. Fly agarics often grow near porcini, and young ones can look like undeveloped boletes. Leave mould-infected specimens in the forest.

name: Black trumpet
description: A fun find, recognised by the black lower stem and the black upper side of the cap.
howToEat: Eat the whole mushroom; best dried as a seasoning mushroom for stocks, soups and crumbled into cream sauces, but also good fried fresh.

harvest.note: often first appears in August or September

foraging.picking: Blue-black and trumpet-shaped, with a narrow stem widening into the cap; not easy to confuse if you look closely. Grows among moss on damp, lime-rich ground.
foraging.habitat: Mossy coniferous and mixed forest, often around hazel, beech or oak.
foraging.distribution: Throughout Sweden, less common in the north.
foraging.identification: Black cap with a grey-blue underside, hollow black stem and a trumpet-shaped body.

lookAlikes.name: Sinuous chanterelle (kruskantarell)
lookAlikes.howToTell: Rare and lighter in colour.

lookAlikes.name: Ashen chanterelle
lookAlikes.howToTell: Has ridges under the cap.

name: Common puffball
notes: Older classifications place puffballs in Lycoperdaceae.
description: The bacon-flavoured common puffball can be more useful than just something to kick for the smoke effect.
howToEat: Eat the whole young, white mushroom fresh: slice small and fry in oil with butter and onion at the end; it turns crisp and tastes like bacon.

foraging.picking: Small, neat and white when picked, often 10-20 together on heaths and clearings. Cut it lengthwise: it must be white throughout, not developed too far. Rub off the warts before putting it in the basket.
foraging.identification: Pear-shaped fruit body with small pointed warts that come off easily when touched.

lookAlikes.name: Young fly agarics (Amanita)
lookAlikes.howToTell: Cut the mushroom in half: puffball flesh is completely white with no pattern, whereas a young amanita shows the outline of gills and the cap skin as a thin coloured line under the surface. If unsure, skip small specimens.

lookAlikes.name: Stump puffball
lookAlikes.howToTell: Edible; has no warts.

foraging.safety: Can be confused with young poisonous fly agarics: always cut it in half to check, and skip small specimens if in any doubt. Only eat puffballs that are pure white inside.

name: Meadowsweet
description: Look for a cloud of insects above creamy white ditch flowers with plumes like feather dusters.
howToEat: Flavour ice cream with the flowers, make cordial or syrup from fresh flowers, or dry them for tea; it has traditionally been used to flavour beer.

foraging.picking: A member of the rose family with a strong, sweet smell. Insects swarm around the feather-duster-like flowers, though it offers no nectar.
foraging.identification: 50-120 cm tall, strongly scented white flowers with five petals; pinnate leaves with toothed, lance-shaped leaflets.

lookAlikes.name: Dropwort
lookAlikes.howToTell: Also edible and also in the rose family.

foraging.safety: Naturally contains salicylic acid (as in headache tablets).

name: Wood hedgehog
description: Besides being really tasty, the best thing about the hedgehog mushroom is that it appears in such large quantities.
howToEat: An all-round meaty mushroom: eat the whole cap pickled, fried or dried. The spines are edible, but can be scraped off in the forest.

foraging.picking: Grows in ordinary Swedish forest, coniferous and mixed, best where it is damp after good rain. Resists insects and lasts well into autumn, often into November. All hedgehog fungi are edible; from above it might be mistaken for a polypore, but the spines underneath tell them apart.
foraging.identification: Cap up to 15 cm, pale white to whitish-yellow with red and yellow tinges, fleshy and matt; brittle, slightly paler pointed spines underneath that may run onto the white stem; white, pleasant-smelling flesh.

lookAlikes.name: Terracotta hedgehog and other hedgehog fungi
lookAlikes.howToTell: Other edible hedgehog fungi; all hedgehog fungi are edible.

lookAlikes.name: Polypores (bracket fungi)
lookAlikes.howToTell: Only similar from directly above; the spines underneath make the difference easy to see.

name: Saffron milkcap
description: A great edible mushroom popular across Europe, and a good milkcap to start with.
howToEat: Eat the whole mushroom fried in butter, perhaps with garlic, alone or with other mushrooms; also good dried or pickled.

foraging.picking: There are pine and spruce forms; the pine one is considered best. It looks grubby and pitted, almost as if attacked. To identify, break off a bit of cap: it bleeds carrot-coloured milk. Where there is one there are usually more.
foraging.identification: Spruce form: orange-red cap, gills and stem, cap sticky when wet, hollow stem. Pine form: orange-red to brick-red cap with concentric rings and darker pits towards the edge; hard, pale red, pitted stem. Both bleed carrot-coloured milk.

lookAlikes.name: Woolly milkcap
lookAlikes.howToTell: Harmless per the book; has a hairy fringe on the underside of the cap that is easy to see.

lookAlikes.name: Fenugreek milkcap
lookAlikes.howToTell: Mildly poisonous; it exudes white milk (not carrot-coloured) and smells of liquorice.

foraging.safety: Beginners should be careful with gilled mushrooms. The fenugreek milkcap is mildly poisonous; check the milk colour.

name: Cauliflower fungus
description: A real jackpot on a mushroom outing is a big specimen of the cauliflower fungus.
howToEat: Split the whole mushroom and break into pieces to shake out bugs, then fry or deep-fry it plain for a crisp texture; mild taste with a hint of pine.

foraging.picking: Fairly rare, almost always growing alone on the roots or lower trunk of a pine. Leave small ones, note the spot and return when bigger. Cut it off close to the tree with a knife to get it in one piece.
foraging.habitat: On or right next to a pine.
foraging.identification: Like a cauliflower head of wavy, ear-like folds; can be 30-40 cm wide and weigh several kilos; pale white to yellow.

lookAlikes.name: Coral fungi
lookAlikes.howToTell: Possibly confused from a distance; up close it has no finger-like branches. The book does not give their edibility.

name: Bay bolete
description: An overlooked bolete with its merits; as an edible mushroom it is not unlike the familiar button mushroom.
howToEat: Eat the whole mushroom fried, used much like a button mushroom; meaty, so also good pickled. Trim off yellowed pores on older specimens.

foraging.picking: Brown cap that feels floury or velvety when young, yellow-brown stem; likes damper ground. Taste a little in the forest: it should be mild; leave bitter boletes behind. Pores yellow with age; trim them off if not pale.
foraging.distribution: Up to central Sweden, rarer further north.
foraging.identification: Yellow pores that bruise blue when pressed; finely velvety when young, later smooth and sticky; stem tapering at the base, mottled yellow-brown; mild smell.

lookAlikes.name: Devil's bolete
lookAlikes.howToTell: Poisonous; it is clearly reddish.

foraging.safety: Can be confused with the poisonous devil's bolete. Leave bitter-tasting boletes in the forest.

name: Sheep polypore
description: Besides being Medelpad's provincial mushroom, the sheep polypore is a good beginner's mushroom with fine food value.
howToEat: Eat the whole mushroom breaded and fried like a vegetarian burger, or cut into pieces as protein in a stew.

foraging.picking: Unlike most polypores it grows on the ground, in large numbers, in mixed forest, clearings and lumpy moss. Often found in quantity and large, so easy to gather a lot. Easily confused with the fused polypore, which has several caps on one stem, but mixing them up is harmless.
foraging.habitat: Mossy coniferous forest, usually by spruce.
foraging.distribution: All of Sweden except the far north and far south.
foraging.identification: White to grey-brown smooth cap; underside completely smooth (fine pores), often in varying yellow shades; pale, smooth stem.

lookAlikes.name: Fused polypore and related Albatrellus (lammticka)
lookAlikes.howToTell: Edible; more orange-brown. The fused polypore grows with several caps on one stem.

lookAlikes.name: Inedible polypore (ängsticka)
lookAlikes.howToTell: Inedible; sulphur-yellow on the underside.

name: Weeping milkcap
description: Its flesh smells of shellfish, making it a striking oddity among the best edible mushrooms.
howToEat: Eat the whole mushroom cooked, when it tastes of shellfish; firm enough to simmer in stews, and good dried and ground into mushroom flour for a fishy note in stock.
