foraging.picking: Grows in coniferous forest from late July to September. Cut the gills with a knife and it bleeds white milk. Recognise it by the stem, almost like a wine cork, and very meaty texture.
foraging.habitat: Deciduous and coniferous forest, often with oak and spruce.
foraging.identification: Orange, yellow-brown to red-brown and compact; fresh gills bleed white milk; strong shellfish smell; cap bruises brown when handled.

lookAlikes.name: Fenugreek milkcap
lookAlikes.howToTell: Mildly poisonous; it has clear (see-through) milk and smells slightly of liquorice.

lookAlikes.name: Other orange milkcaps (rävriska, brandriska)
lookAlikes.howToTell: Smaller and more brittle, without the shellfish smell; the book does not give their edibility.

foraging.safety: The most likely look-alike, the fenugreek milkcap, is mildly poisonous.

name: Oyster mushroom
description: A lovely edible mushroom, also sold cultivated in shops.
howToEat: Slice the whole mushroom and fry thoroughly, adding butter and onion once the liquid has cooked off; can be dried but is best fresh.

foraging.picking: Grows on trees, often dead deciduous ones, attached by a small white stem, usually in clusters. Not very common, but often returns to the same spot; quantities are seldom large.
foraging.habitat: Tree trunks, roots and damaged stumps.
foraging.distribution: All of Sweden, less common in the north.
foraging.identification: Grey-brown (or grey-blue) cap with a short, off-centre stem; usually on deciduous trees, sometimes on conifers.

lookAlikes.name: Veiled oyster (ringmussling)
lookAlikes.howToTell: Easily confused; not dangerous but not tasty either.

lookAlikes.name: Broskmussling
lookAlikes.howToTell: Tougher and inedible, but not poisonous.

lookAlikes.name: Pale oyster
lookAlikes.howToTell: Same food value as the oyster mushroom.

name: English oak
description: One of the forest's mightiest trees has nuts for anyone not put off by bitterness; acorns are good for more than emergency food.
howToEat: Leach the acorns by boiling in several changes of water (or roasting) to remove tannin, then use for flour in baking and pancakes, flavour ice cream, candy roasted acorns, or as a coffee substitute.

foraging.picking: Mainly the acorn is used. Fresh acorns are very bitter from tannin, and bitterness seems to vary between trees, so compare a few peeled green acorns. The landowner's permission is needed to pick acorns.
foraging.distribution: From southern Sweden up to the Dalälven river.
foraging.identification: The leaf shape and the acorns.

lookAlikes.name: Sessile oak
lookAlikes.howToTell: Similar oak; the book does not describe how to tell them apart.

foraging.safety: Raw acorns are full of bitter tannin; leach before eating. Landowner permission is required.

name: Cranberry
description: Not good fresh, but brilliant processed into an ice-cold thirst-quencher on a hot summer day.
howToEat: Use the berries dried or fresh in chutney, jam and above all cordial; dried in granola or on porridge. They contain natural benzoic acid, so no preservative is needed.

harvest.note: best after the first frost or in early spring

foraging.picking: Grows on bogs like cloudberries, with berries seemingly sitting on the ground, about the size of a large cultivated blueberry. Bitter and sour: pick after the first frost, or wait until early spring for sweeter berries.
foraging.distribution: Common in almost the whole country, less so in the mountains and on Öland and Gotland.
foraging.identification: Large berries growing close to the ground.

lookAlikes.name: Small cranberry
lookAlikes.howToTell: Same food value.

foraging.safety: Avoid if taking the blood thinner warfarin, as substances in the berries counteract the drug.

name: Winter chanterelle
description: Rightly one of Swedes' real favourite mushrooms: flavourful, with a fine texture, and luckily not rare at all.
howToEat: Eat the whole mushroom fried fresh (crisp and chewy) or pickled then fried; great for stock, and dries well (soak before use or grind to powder, using sparingly).

foraging.picking: A late autumn mushroom, slender, with a hollow pale yellow stem up to a light brown cap and forked ridges underneath, in large stands in damp mossy conifer forest. Pick carefully so no deadly webcap, which can grow right alongside, gets into the basket.
foraging.distribution: All of Sweden except the far north of Norrland.
foraging.identification: Hollow brownish-yellow to yellow stem; thin, funnel-shaped cap, yellow-brown to brown-black on top.

lookAlikes.name: Jelly baby (slemmurkling)
lookAlikes.howToTell: Bad-tasting; lacks the trumpet shape and feels and looks jelly-like.

lookAlikes.name: Golden chanterelle (rödgul trumpetsvamp)
lookAlikes.howToTell: A fine edible mushroom.

lookAlikes.name: Deadly webcap
lookAlikes.howToTell: Really poisonous and can grow side by side with winter chanterelles. It has a pointed cap without the trumpet shape and brown gills under the cap; be very wary of any mushroom brown in both gills and cap.

foraging.safety: The deadly webcap can grow among winter chanterelles: pick each mushroom carefully and reject anything with brown gills and a brown pointed cap.

name: Common juniper
description: Fresh, young juniper berries have more to offer than the dried ones in the shop.
howToEat: Use green second-year or ripe berries whole or crushed with game, in meat rubs or juniper salt; branches with berries for juniper drink; needles for pickling brine, and needles and branches for smoking.

harvest.note: berries take three years to ripen; all stages usable

foraging.picking: Common throughout the country. Berries ripen over three years (grey-white, green, then blue-black). Pick after rain when less prickly, or wear gloves; knock ripe berries onto a cloth, pick other stages by hand. Landowner permission needed for berries or branches.
foraging.identification: Sharp, prickly needles, blue-green above and darker below; berry-like cones.

lookAlikes.name: Other junipers
lookAlikes.howToTell: All can be used the same way.

foraging.safety: Landowner permission is required to harvest berries or branches.

name: Star-tipped reindeer lichen
description: A lichen that deserves better than decorating candlesticks; top chefs have started singing its praises.
howToEat: Soak briefly, clean out needles, then fry or deep-fry the whole lichen until crisp, e.g. seasoned with spruce salt, as a crouton substitute.

foraging.picking: Find it on rock outcrops in the forest. Pick on wet days when it is easiest to handle, using two hands so you take only the part above ground. Take only what you need, as it grows slowly. Recognised by its ball shape, unlike finger-like lichens.
foraging.distribution: Common throughout Sweden except the far south.
foraging.identification: Branching stems forming a bushy, cushion-like shape.

lookAlikes.name: Other lichens
lookAlikes.howToTell: Star-tipped reindeer lichen forms round, cushion-like balls rather than upright finger-like stalks.

foraging.safety: Never eat shop-bought decorative lichen, which is reportedly treated with flame retardant. Harvest sparingly; it grows slowly.

name: Crowberry
description: A tart, overlooked berry that quenches thirst and can be used for anything from cordial and wine to desserts.
howToEat: Use the berries for jelly, jam, cordial and traditionally wine, or eat fresh as a dessert berry; they keep for weeks in the fridge.

foraging.picking: Pick by hand, or use a berry picker for larger amounts if you don't mind cleaning afterwards. Tart and not very sweet, good as a base for thirst-quenchers.
foraging.habitat: Poor ground, bare mountains, heaths, bogs and clearings.
foraging.identification: Black berries and needle-like leaves on an evergreen dwarf shrub; hard to confuse when berries are present, resembling heather with short needles.

name: Common polypody
description: A piece of polypody root in your mouth takes you straight back to childhood adventures in the forest.
howToEat: Use the root, fresh or dried: grate fresh over strawberries for a sweet liquorice note, candy it, or steep dried root in hot water for tea; peeling makes it less bitter.

foraging.picking: A fern common in rocky forest on outcrops and mossy stones. Only the root is used. Ease the brittle root out of the soil with your fingers, snip off the fronds, then soak and brush clean at home.
foraging.identification: 10-40 cm tall with pinnately lobed fronds growing directly from the rootstock; undersides dotted with round spore clusters.

lookAlikes.name: Other ferns
lookAlikes.howToTell: Some are poisonous. Check for the round spore dots under the fronds and fronds growing directly from the creeping rootstock on mossy rocks.

foraging.safety: Some other ferns are poisonous, so identify carefully. Don't eat too much: it gets very bitter and contains a substance that in large amounts breaks down vitamin B1.

name: Scots pine
description: Shoots, cones and needles: the pine has plenty to offer, from cone marmalade to pine salt.
howToEat: Pickle whole young shoots in brine (they taste of chai and raspberry); boil green cones into syrup or marmalade; make needle tea, or dry and grind needles into salt and spice blends.

harvest.note: young annual shoots; timing not stated in book

foraging.picking: The young annual shoots are the highlight: tap off the brown husk while still on the branch. Green cones and needles can also be used. Take only a couple of cones or shoots per tree, and ask the landowner first.
foraging.identification: Long needles and scent, straight trunk and sparse crown.

lookAlikes.name: Cultivated pine species
lookAlikes.howToTell: The book does not describe how to tell them apart.

foraging.safety: Take only a couple of cones or shoots per tree, and ask the landowner's permission.

name: Common chickweed
description: Like many plants it is usually called a weed, but it is pleasant in food and nutritious too.
howToEat: Use the leafy tops fresh in salads (flowers too), like spinach, or in pesto and green smoothies; mild, grassy taste. Not worth pickling or drying.

foraging.picking: A very common weed, green all year, forming lawn-sized stands, easiest found in gardens. Recognised by the line of hairs along one side of the stem. Grab the middle of the plant and cut below your hand with scissors; the upper half is tender.
foraging.identification: 5-30 cm tall, growing loosely in large stands; broad oval leaves, small white flowers and a line of fine hairs along the brittle stem.
foraging.safety: The book notes a small risk of confusion with poisonous plants (none named), so identify carefully.

name: Hairy bittercress
description: A peppery, slightly hairy cabbage-family plant with a cress-like taste that flowers in spring and likes the coast.
howToEat: Leaves, flowers, seeds and shoots go in salads or as seasoning; add it to hot dishes just before serving so it keeps its peppery taste.

foraging.picking: Common on stony and gravelly ground; it grows all season and is often treated as a weed.
foraging.habitat: Rock outcrops, gravel, shore banks and forest edges.
foraging.distribution: Along the coast up to central Sweden.
foraging.identification: A basal rosette of paired leaflets (up to seven pairs), a few hairy stem leaves and small white flowers.

lookAlikes.name: Other bittercresses (large bitter-cress, wavy bittercress)
lookAlikes.howToTell: They grow in different habitats; all bittercresses are edible.

name: Birch
description: We may not think of birch as food, but both the sap and the leaves are nice to use in the kitchen.
howToEat: Drink the sap fresh, ferment it with apples or boil it into syrup; small waxy young leaves are sweet and good in desserts, older leaves can be fermented for tea.

harvest.note: young 'mouse ears' to eat; older leaves for tea

foraging.picking: Tap sap in spring before leaf-out: drill a hole, insert a tube into a covered container, tap for about a day, then seal the hole with a carved plug and some moss. Chaga (a black parasitic growth) can be found on birch for tea.
foraging.identification: Silver-white bark with black markings; downy birch has smooth bark, silver birch rough bark at the base of the trunk. Dwarf birch is much smaller.
foraging.safety: Only tap sap before the leaves burst, for the tree's sake; afterwards it needs the sap itself. Plug the hole afterwards.

name: Stinging nettle
description: Nettle offers greens all season, and the brave can put tiny young shoots on a dessert as a tingling surprise.
howToEat: Young shoots and leaves are classic in nettle soup; very young shoots can even be used fresh in desserts. Dried seed capsules go in muesli.

foraging.picking: Pick shoots from a few centimetres up to plants about 10-20 cm tall; leaves can be picked until seed sets, then take the seed capsules. Wear work gloves.
foraging.habitat: Ditches, meadows, flower beds and grassland.
foraging.identification: Stinging hairs on leaves and stem; opposite, pointed egg-shaped leaves with serrated edges.

lookAlikes.name: Small nettle
lookAlikes.howToTell: Appears somewhat later in the season and has the same food value.

lookAlikes.name: White and red dead-nettle
lookAlikes.howToTell: Look like nettle before flowering but lack stinging hairs; also edible.

foraging.safety: Stinging hairs can cause blisters; wear gloves. Avoid fertilised land to limit nitrate intake.

name: Lady's mantle
description: Lady's mantle is best known as a styptic medicinal herb, but it also suits salads.
howToEat: Leaves (about 5 cm across) are a mild filler mixed with nettle or ground elder; the yellow flowers are edible and the plant traditionally makes a tasty tea.

foraging.picking: Easy to spot by the cup-shaped leaves that collect water drops. Cut with scissors below the leaf base; it grows in large stands. Leave the stem in the ground to regrow.
foraging.habitat: Lawns and meadows, some species also in forest.
foraging.identification: 10-30 cm tall with large, almost round leaves with toothed lobes and small light green flowers.

lookAlikes.name: Other lady's mantle species
lookAlikes.howToTell: There are about 20 species in Sweden and all are usable.

name: Norway spruce
description: Spruce is good for more than Christmas decoration: needles and shoots bring the forest straight into your kitchen.
howToEat: Pickle young shoots for meat or desserts, or make cordial, syrup and jam; pickle the red female flowers; blend mature needles with salt into spruce salt.

foraging.picking: Pinch off the shoots while they are still glossy and not prickly; timing depends on how much sun the tree gets. Needles can be picked all year.
foraging.identification: Conical evergreen tree with single, pointed, fragrant needles.

lookAlikes.name: Yew
lookAlikes.howToTell: Do not use yew: it has red berry-like seeds and flat needles. Spruce has pointed needles and its red flowers are not berries.

foraging.safety: Do not take too many shoots from each tree and get the landowner's permission. Yew is poisonous.

name: Cowslip
description: A pretty little flower that turns up in the lawn but also suits the plate.
howToEat: The mildly floral, sweet flowers are lovely fresh as garnish or in salads; they can also be candied, used to flavour water, or dried for spice blends and tea.

foraging.picking: One of the early spring flowers in meadows and lawns, with slightly rough hairy leaves and elongated bell-shaped flowers on the stalk. Protected; see safety.
foraging.habitat: Meadows and grassland, preferably lime-rich soil.
foraging.identification: Toothed leaves, leafless stalk topped by a cluster of yellow flowers.

lookAlikes.name: Oxlip
lookAlikes.howToTell: Has larger flowers and leaves that taper evenly.

foraging.safety: Protected throughout Sweden: picking is banned entirely in Halland, Skåne and Örebro counties; elsewhere only for household use, leaving the root in the ground.

name: Bitter vetch
description: A beautiful early spring flower with a fine pea-like taste, found mainly in meadows.
howToEat: The flowers have a pea-like taste and good bite; use them fresh in salads or as garnish. The plant itself is woody; the root is said to be edible too.

foraging.picking: Grows in forest and meadows, often in large stands, frequently alongside meadowsweet. Flowers vary in violet and pink with different veining; leave the seed pods on the plant.
foraging.identification: Usually only 2-3 pairs of leaflets, no tendrils, winged stems, pink to pale violet flowers in few-flowered clusters.

lookAlikes.name: Spring pea
lookAlikes.howToTell: Has more oval leaves; the book says confusing it with other pea plants is no danger.

name: Wood sorrel
description: It is almost impossible not to stop and eat a handful of wood sorrel when you come across it in the forest.
howToEat: The citrusy sour leaves and white flowers suit desserts, ice cream and noodle salads.

foraging.picking: Spreads like a carpet of clover-like leaves that fold up in rain or evening. A perennial with creeping rhizome; the white flowers appear in early May.
foraging.habitat: Natural ground, preferably moist; mixed forest.
foraging.distribution: All of Sweden except the far north of Norrland and the mountains.
foraging.identification: Three heart-shaped leaflets; green leaf stalk turning red.

lookAlikes.name: Wood anemone
lookAlikes.howToTell: Its flowers resemble wood sorrel's. Wood sorrel flowers have white stamens and pink veins.

foraging.safety: Contains oxalic acid: large amounts can irritate the gut and people with kidney stones should avoid it. Flowers resemble the poisonous wood anemone.

name: Water avens
description: Nodding flowers that look nice in salads, and a root you can boil into a chocolate-like drink.
howToEat: Use fresh young shoots and flowers in salads; peeled roots steeped in hot water for 20-30 minutes, then sweetened with sugar and warm milk, make a chocolate-like drink.

foraging.picking: Look in wet meadows and ditch edges; it rarely grows in large stands. Dig roots early in spring while they are still sweet.
foraging.habitat: Moist ground, meadows, ditches and fens.
foraging.identification: Nodding bell-shaped flower with a velvety hairy calyx; three-fingered stem leaves and pinnate basal leaves with a large end leaflet.

lookAlikes.name: Wood avens
lookAlikes.howToTell: Has yellow flowers.

name: Bird cherry
description: Bird cherry has a hint of bitter almond and flowers lavishly in May; the berries ripening in August are called 'poor man's cherries' in Norrland.
howToEat: Use the flowers fresh or pickled as edible decoration or make cordial; the sweet but very astringent berries make wine or flavoured vinegar.

foraging.picking: Pick the flowers quickly while in bloom. The small black berries come in August; like rowan, wait until after frost.
foraging.habitat: Moist soil, groves and lake shores.
foraging.distribution: All of Sweden except Öland and Gotland; a northern subspecies is more common in the mountains.
foraging.identification: Oval serrated leaves, black berries, small white flowers in clusters.

lookAlikes.name: Goat willow
lookAlikes.howToTell: Look for bird cherry's serrated leaves.

foraging.safety: The bark contains the poison amygdalin. The berries have a stone, so bite carefully.

name: Ground ivy
description: A dainty little plant that is pleasantly spicy, perfect to sprinkle over food as a herb.
howToEat: Stems, leaves and flowers are aromatic; chop fresh and sprinkle over food, or use like thyme in stews and sauces, even as an accent in desserts.

foraging.picking: Snip just above the ground; the whole stem with leaves and flowers is usable. Rubbed leaves smell of thyme and mint. Prefers milder climates.
foraging.distribution: Southern and central Sweden, less in the north.
foraging.identification: Violet or purple flowers, aromatic scent, stalked leaves with kidney-shaped base and scalloped edges.

lookAlikes.name: Mints and red dead-nettle
lookAlikes.howToTell: The book describes them as harmless.

name: Ground elder
description: Start eating the ground elder in your garden and you won't curse it, just make sure it isn't a poisonous cousin.
howToEat: Use leaves like spinach: young leaves fresh in salads, fried, in soups, smoothies or creamed. Small plants with glossy leaves taste best; it gets more bitter as it grows.

foraging.picking: Forms large stands. Pinch off at ground level and rinse off soil in cold water. Recognise it by once or twice three-fingered leaves with broad, pointed, toothed leaflets.
foraging.distribution: Common on cultivated land throughout the country, rarer in the mountains.
foraging.identification: 30-100 cm, angular grooved stem, once or twice three-fingered leaves that are broad, pointed and toothed; small white flowers in umbels.

lookAlikes.name: Cowbane
lookAlikes.howToTell: Belongs to the same umbellifer family; it is important to rule out these dangerous plants before picking.

lookAlikes.name: Fool's parsley
lookAlikes.howToTell: Same family; must be ruled out before picking.

lookAlikes.name: Hemlock
lookAlikes.howToTell: Same family; must be ruled out before picking.

lookAlikes.name: Masterwort
lookAlikes.howToTell: Its leaves resemble ground elder's; the book calls it harmless.

foraging.safety: Ground elder is an umbellifer: rule out the dangerous relatives cowbane, fool's parsley and hemlock.

name: Orpine
description: Orpine is a favourite of the author's children, who love eating it out foraging.
howToEat: Eat the crunchy, juicy leaves raw as a trail snack; larger stems can be lightly blanched like asparagus. The flowers are bitter and not eaten.

foraging.picking: Grows on rock outcrops and slopes, often with polypody. Pick the leaves until flowering; stems get harder as the plant grows.
foraging.habitat: Rocks, stony slopes and dry ground.
foraging.identification: Fleshy leaves. Wild plants have white or yellow-green flowers; pink-red ones in the wild are a naturalised subspecies.

name: Shepherd's purse
description: Don't miss the mustard and ginger flavour of this otherwise rather unremarkable plant.
howToEat: Everything except the root is edible: flowers as garnish, the heart-shaped seed pods fresh or dried with a ginger-mustard taste, and stems infused in oil.

foraging.picking: Recognised by its slender stem with white flowers on top and small triangular, almost heart-shaped pods along the stem. Snip at ground level.
foraging.habitat: Cultivated land and typical weed habitats.
foraging.distribution: All of Sweden except the mountains.
foraging.identification: 15-30 cm tall, leaves almost only at the base, heart-shaped seed pods and white flowers.

lookAlikes.name: Field pennycress
lookAlikes.howToTell: Does not have heart-shaped seed pods.

name: Sweet violet
description: A classic, very fragrant flower that tastes as much as it smells.
howToEat: Candy the flowers for desserts, or use them for cordial or to flavour cream, panna cotta or ice cream; the slightly sour leaves suit salads.

foraging.picking: Found in meadows; purple flowers with three lower and two upper petals and a sweet floral scent. Pick the whole stem, as leaves are edible too.
foraging.identification: 10-15 cm tall, kidney- to heart-shaped leaves slightly hairy underneath; strongly scented flowers.

lookAlikes.name: Other violets
lookAlikes.howToTell: All can be used the same way.

name: Garlic mustard
notes: Biennial in the wild.
description: With both garlic and mustard flavour in one plant, garlic mustard is a pleasant acquaintance.
howToEat: Use leaves fresh as a garlic substitute in salads, garnishes and vinaigrettes (flavour fades when dried or cooked); the radish-like root is eaten early in the season.

foraging.picking: A biennial that flowers in its second year. The whole plant is edible, so pick it whole including the root; it travels well in a paper bag or basket.
foraging.habitat: Thrives in gardens and is often called a weed.
foraging.distribution: Southern and central Sweden, very common in the Mälaren valley.
foraging.identification: Smells and tastes of onion/garlic; large heart-shaped leaves; can grow up to a metre tall.

name: Dandelion
description: According to the Swedish army, dandelion is one of the fourteen most important plants in a survival situation.
howToEat: Leaves suit salads (soak in cold water overnight to reduce bitterness); flowers make syrup or wine, buds can be pickled, and roots flavour gratin or are dried for flour.

foraging.picking: Grows almost everywhere and the whole plant from root to flower is usable. Pull up whole plants with roots only on your own land.
foraging.habitat: Lawns, meadows, flower beds and roadsides.
foraging.distribution: All of Sweden except the bare mountains.
foraging.identification: Leafless stem, yellow flowers, lobed leaves; bleeds white sap.

lookAlikes.name: Chicory
lookAlikes.howToTell: Edible.

lookAlikes.name: Other dandelion species
lookAlikes.howToTell: All are edible.

foraging.safety: Dig up whole plants only on your own land.

name: Sweet woodruff
description: Sweet woodruff is often found with the nose rather than the eyes.
howToEat: Stems, leaves and flowers flavour May wine or replace cinnamon in buns when dried and ground; use as a spice. Woody older plants can be fried in butter with apple.

foraging.picking: On warm, dry days the scent of vanilla and fresh hay carries; follow it. Cut the plant at ground level and leave the roots.
foraging.identification: 10-30 cm tall, smooth stem with whorls of 6-8 long leaves, small white flowers at the top.

lookAlikes.name: Other plants
lookAlikes.howToTell: The distinct scent, especially of young plants, confirms you have the right species.

foraging.safety: Contains coumarin, which is mildly toxic; use it as a spice and flavouring, not in large amounts.

name: Bog myrtle
description: Bog myrtle is a classic spirit flavouring and a natural mosquito repellent; picking leaves a strong scent on your hands.
howToEat: Use the leaves and twigs to flavour schnapps or stews; the taste is distinctive, herbal, perfumed and slightly bitter.

harvest.note: the author picks from June until October

foraging.picking: Grows along shores and around lakes; snip off the thin branches and take whole twigs home.
foraging.habitat: Shores, bogs and along watercourses in moist ground.
foraging.distribution: Skåne to central Sweden, also along the Norrland coast.
foraging.identification: Aromatic shrub just over a metre tall with leaves that have a clear midrib.

lookAlikes.name: Bog bilberry
lookAlikes.howToTell: Similar before flowering, but bog myrtle stands out by its scent.

name: Warty cabbage
description: An aromatic, fragrant cabbage-family plant that is particularly common in Uppland.
howToEat: Eat young leaves like kale, fresh with oil and vinegar or lightly blanched; use flowers as decoration or blend them into flower sugar.

foraging.picking: A ditch plant over a metre tall that flowers in June-July, smells strongly floral and grows in large stands, so large amounts are easy to pick.
foraging.distribution: Most common in Uppland, also in some southern and central Swedish provinces.
foraging.identification: Aromatic scent, yellow flowers and long pointed leaves.

lookAlikes.name: Winter cress
lookAlikes.howToTell: Can be used the same way; it has smaller, rounder leaves.

name: Wych elm
description: Don't miss the elm seeds in early summer, a fine early delicacy dressed with apple cider vinegar or browned butter.
howToEat: Eat the crisp, nutty coin-shaped fruits fresh in salads with cider vinegar, infuse them in oil or toss in browned butter; leaves can go in salads too.

foraging.picking: Be quick in early summer: the coin-like fruits soon fall. They hang in large bunches that are easy to harvest.
foraging.habitat: Broadleaf forest; often planted in parks.
foraging.identification: Rough, pointed leaves with lopsided base; coin-shaped fruits in bunches.

lookAlikes.name: Other elm species
lookAlikes.howToTell: The book only names them as look-alikes.

name: Winter cress
description: Evergreen winter cress is a cabbage-family plant with a cress flavour, much like warty cabbage.
howToEat: Leaves and small yellow flowers are peppery and slightly bitter; flowers garnish salads, and before flowering the whole stem can be lightly blanched.

foraging.picking: Grows in meadows and along roads; lower than warty cabbage with shorter, rounder leaves. Cut some way down the stem.
foraging.identification: 30-80 cm tall with many smooth glossy leaves and small yellow flowers.

lookAlikes.name: Warty cabbage
lookAlikes.howToTell: Edible.

lookAlikes.name: Charlock
lookAlikes.howToTell: Edible.

name: Lilac
description: A beautiful burst of perfume that is as good candied as in a vase on the table.
howToEat: The sturdy flowers can be candied (egg white then sugar), made into lilac sugar or cordial, dried, or used fresh as garnish; match the food to the strong perfume.

foraging.picking: Cut just at the base of the flower cluster with herb scissors and shake off insects before putting it in the basket.
foraging.distribution: Southern to central Sweden and up along the Norrland coast.
foraging.identification: The scent and large flower clusters; ovate, pointed, smooth leaves.

name: Rowan
description: Berries from different rowan trees can taste very different, so try several.
howToEat: Dry young leaves for a mildly vanilla tea; berries are classic in jelly and can be salted or pickled, e.g. salted rowanberries with game.

foraging.picking: Pick berries at the first frost, as they are very bitter before; or freeze them for a while. Leave berries on the tree for winter birds.
foraging.distribution: Common throughout Sweden; a northern subspecies occurs mostly in the mountains.
foraging.identification: Smooth grey bark, large red berry clusters, pinnate leaves with 6-8 pairs of sharply toothed leaflets.
foraging.safety: Leave some berries for the birds.

name: Chicken of the woods
description: The meaty, tasty and debated sulphur shelf is called 'chicken of the woods' in the USA.
howToEat: Its texture makes it very good fried; blanch it before further cooking to be on the safe side.

foraging.picking: Grows on tree trunks, usually oak. Grip firmly and break or cut it off; trim the hard part nearest the trunk. Choose young specimens, as old ones get bitter and woody.
foraging.identification: Grows on trunks, sulphur-yellow colour, relatively soft texture.
foraging.safety: Its edibility is debated, including whether it may contain hallucinogens when eaten raw; blanch before cooking.

name: Black morel
description: A rather rare delicacy that must not be confused with its poisonous cousin, the false morel.
howToEat: Excellent fried, on toast or creamed; best fresh, though drying and pickling also work. Parboil twice for 5 minutes first.

foraging.picking: Short season in May-June; often found around clear-cuts among bark and brushwood. Grows sparsely, usually 10-15 cm tall.
foraging.habitat: Deciduous and coniferous forest, clear-cuts, pastures and meadows.
foraging.distribution: Recorded across Sweden, mostly in central Sweden.
foraging.identification: Brown, pointed, hollow cap with a ridged surface of small cell-like pits; white hollow stem.

lookAlikes.name: False morel
lookAlikes.howToTell: Now considered poisonous even after parboiling. Its cap is convoluted differently, not ridged into chambers, and is more lumpy and coarser in shape.

foraging.safety: Parboil twice for 5 minutes and discard the water each time, as it could be confused with the poisonous false morel.

name: Daisy
description: Daisies grow by the thousand in lawns and parks and make excellent edible decoration.
howToEat: The flowers add little flavour but a mild herbal note, crunch and good looks as garnish; young leaves are edible too.

foraging.picking: Grows in large numbers in lawns until the snow. Buds can be picked but open by the time you get home; leaves are best young in early spring.
foraging.identification: White or white-red flowers on a leafless stem.

name: White dead-nettle
description: Perhaps you sucked nectar from a white dead-nettle flower as a child; if not, now is the time.
howToEat: Use leaves like nettle but milder, good for bulking out nettles; the nectar-sweet flowers make garnish or a sweet, toffee-like tea.

foraging.picking: Before flowering it resembles nettle but lacks stinging hairs. Flowers May-September in whorls; perennial, 20-60 cm, often in large stands. Red dead-nettle works just as well.
foraging.habitat: Cultivated land, in dense stands by roads, streets and walls.
foraging.distribution: Common in eastern Sweden far up into Norrland; rarer inland and in the west.
foraging.identification: 20-60 cm tall, hollow stem, dark green toothed leaves, white two-lipped flowers in whorls.

lookAlikes.name: Red dead-nettle
lookAlikes.howToTell: Used the same way.

lookAlikes.name: Stinging nettle
lookAlikes.howToTell: Has stinging hairs; also edible.

name: Yellow star-of-Bethlehem
description: This wild onion relative flowers as early as April-May and is both flavourful and decorative.
howToEat: Use the whole plant except the root in salads or as garnish, stems like spring onion, flowers as decoration; can be blanched briefly.

foraging.picking: Often appears in gardens and lawns; pick at 10-15 cm. The whole plant withers after flowering.
foraging.distribution: Southern Sweden to Uppland, rare further north.
foraging.identification: Broad grey-green basal leaf, bare flower stalks with umbrella-like clusters on top; only one new side bulb inside the bulb skin.

lookAlikes.name: Meadow gagea
lookAlikes.howToTell: Relatively rare and edible; larger flowers, bluer-green basal leaf, several side bulbs outside the skin.

name: Common sorrel
description: Fresh sour flavours are always welcome in food, and common sorrel is one of the hardier kinds.
howToEat: Use the sour leaves in sorrel soup, granita, sorrel salt or as garnish; best fresh but can be dried.

foraging.picking: Easy to find in meadows in spring before the grass grows tall. Pinch off whole leaves at the stem; leaves have two lobes at the base like tailcoat tails.
foraging.distribution: Throughout Sweden; a mountain subspecies is more common in the mountains.
foraging.identification: Small red-brown flowers in clusters along the stem.

lookAlikes.name: Sheep's sorrel
lookAlikes.howToTell: Smaller but also edible.
